scenarios.title: Who ate the disk?
scenarios.summary: The disk alert fired. Find the table that is using the most space.
scenarios.description:
The disk on the `shop` database server is filling up and the on-call channel is asking
**which table is to blame**.

Find the table in database `shop` that uses the most disk space **in total**:
heap + indexes + TOAST, in any schema.

Write its name to `/var/lib/postgresql/solution` (your home directory), as `schema.table`
or just `table`, e.g. `echo public.customers > ~/solution`.
hints: `psql -d shop`, then `\\dt+` is a start, but it only shows schemas on your `search_path`. Try `\\dt+ *.*`.
Heap size is not total size. Compare `pg_relation_size()` with `pg_total_relation_size()`.

`select oid::regclass, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(oid)) from pg_class where relkind='r' and relnamespace::regnamespace::text not in ('pg_catalog','information_schema') order by pg_total_relation_size(oid) desc limit 5;`
scenarios.solution:
`\dt+` only lists `public`, where `audit_log` looks biggest. But there is an `archive` schema,
and `archive.events` stores large values out of line in its **TOAST** table, which `\dt+` and
`pg_relation_size()` don't count.

```sql
select oid::regclass as table,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid))        as heap,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(oid))  as total
from pg_class
where relkind = 'r'
  and relnamespace::regnamespace::text not in ('pg_catalog','information_schema')
order by pg_total_relation_size(oid) desc
limit 5;
```
```
echo archive.events > ~/solution
```
**Lesson:** "table size" means three things (heap, + indexes, + TOAST). Know which one you are quoting.

scenarios.title: A cluster of your own
scenarios.summary: Build Parcelpoint's new cluster from nothing: initdb, sane auth, an owner role and an app role.
scenarios.description:
The box has PostgreSQL 17 installed and **no cluster**. Build one to the spec in `~/README.md`:

1. A cluster in **`/srv/pg/node1`** on **port 5432**, with **data checksums** on, listening on **localhost only**,
   `shared_buffers = 256MB`. Keep the Unix socket in `/var/run/postgresql` (the default).
2. **No `trust`** (and no clear-text `password`) lines in `pg_hba.conf`. Local socket logins for `postgres` stay possible.
3. Database **`parcels`** (UTF8), owned by a **non-login** role **`parcels_owner`**.
4. Login role **`parcels_app`** (password `Parcel-App-2026`, SCRAM) that can connect to `parcels` over
   TCP (`127.0.0.1`) and **create tables in schema `app`**. It is not a superuser and doesn't own the database.

Run the server with `sudo systemctl start postgresql@node1`. The grader restarts it, so settings must be in the config, not just `SET`.
hints: `initdb --help`: look at `--data-checksums`, `--auth-local` and `--auth-host`. Without them initdb configures `trust` for every local connection (it even warns you).
Settings go in `/srv/pg/node1/postgresql.conf` (or `ALTER SYSTEM`, which writes `postgresql.auto.conf`): `port`, `listen_addresses = 'localhost'`, `shared_buffers`. `shared_buffers` needs a restart.
Since PostgreSQL 15 nobody but the database owner can create objects in `public`. Make a schema `app` owned by `parcels_owner` and `GRANT USAGE, CREATE ON SCHEMA app TO parcels_app`.
Check your `pg_hba.conf` the way the server sees it: `SELECT type, database, user_name, address, auth_method FROM pg_hba_file_rules;`
scenarios.solution:
```bash
initdb -D /srv/pg/node1 --data-checksums -E UTF8 --locale=C.UTF-8 --auth-local=peer --auth-host=scram-sha-256
cat >> /srv/pg/node1/postgresql.conf <<'CONF'
port = 5432
listen_addresses = 'localhost'
shared_buffers = 256MB
CONF
sudo systemctl start postgresql@node1
node1 <<'SQL'
CREATE ROLE parcels_owner NOLOGIN;
CREATE ROLE parcels_app LOGIN PASSWORD 'Parcel-App-2026';
CREATE DATABASE parcels OWNER parcels_owner ENCODING 'UTF8';
\c parcels
CREATE SCHEMA app AUTHORIZATION parcels_owner;
GRANT USAGE, CREATE ON SCHEMA app TO parcels_app;
SQL
PGPASSWORD=Parcel-App-2026 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U parcels_app -d parcels -c 'CREATE TABLE app.hello (id int)'
```
**Lesson:** a bare `initdb` gives you `trust` authentication (anyone on the box is any user, including the
superuser) and no checksums. Decide auth at initdb time with `--auth-local=peer --auth-host=scram-sha-256`.
Turn on checksums so silent disk corruption is detected (and so `pg_rewind` works later without `wal_log_hints`).
Separate the **owner** of the data (a role nobody logs in as) from the **app login**, and grant the app exactly
what it needs. Since PostgreSQL 15, `public` is no longer a free-for-all, so give the app its own schema.
scenarios.narrative:
**Dana:** Before you touch the old server, show me what *right* looks like. Here's an empty box. I want a cluster
I'd be happy to put customer data on: checksums, no `trust` anywhere, a database the app doesn't own, and an app
login that can create its own tables and nothing more.

**Tomás:** Last time I just ran `initdb` and it worked fine? 🙂

**Dana:** That's what worries me.

scenarios.title: It won't start
scenarios.summary: After a config change and a restore, Postgres refuses to come up.
scenarios.description:
A colleague tuned the server and restored a file-level copy of the data directory over the
weekend. Now PostgreSQL **won't start**.

Get PostgreSQL running and accepting connections, **without losing data**: database `inventory`
must still have its rows. Don't re-`initdb`.

Start it with `pg_ctl -D $PGDATA -l /var/log/postgresql/postgresql.log start`.
hints: Always read the log first: `tail -n 30 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql.log`.
There is more than one problem. Fix one, try again, read the log again.
Postgres is strict about who can read the data directory. Compare `ls -ld $PGDATA` with what the log says is allowed.
scenarios.solution:
Two problems, one at a time, each found in the log.

1. `invalid value for parameter "shared_buffers": "128MBB"` — a typo in `postgresql.conf`.
   ```
   grep -n shared_buffers $PGDATA/postgresql.conf $PGDATA/postgresql.auto.conf
   ```
   It was set in **`postgresql.auto.conf`** (written by `ALTER SYSTEM`), which overrides `postgresql.conf`.
   Fix the unit (`128MB`) or delete that line.
2. `data directory "/srv/pgdata" has invalid permissions` — the restore left it `0755`.
   ```
   chmod 700 $PGDATA
   ```
Then `pg_ctl -D $PGDATA -l /var/log/postgresql/postgresql.log start` and `psql -d inventory -c 'select count(*) from items'`.

**Lesson:** read the log, fix one thing at a time, and remember `postgresql.auto.conf` wins over `postgresql.conf`.

scenarios.title: Off the hackathon server
scenarios.summary: Upgrade production from PostgreSQL 16 to 17 with pg_upgrade, without losing data, extensions or plans.
scenarios.description:
**`node1`** (`/srv/pg/node1`, port 5432) runs **PostgreSQL 16** with the `parcels` database. The app is stopped
for the maintenance window. Upgrade it to **PostgreSQL 17** with `pg_upgrade`:

1. When you're done, **PostgreSQL 17** answers on **port 5432** with all of `parcels`: every row, the
   `pg_trgm` search index and the `pg_stat_statements` view working.
2. The old 16 server stays **stopped**.
3. `parcels_app` logs in over TCP with its **existing password**. No `trust` in the new `pg_hba.conf`.
4. The planner has **statistics** for the upgraded tables (PostgreSQL 17's `pg_upgrade` doesn't carry them).

Put the new cluster in `/srv/pg/node2` (`postgresql@nodeN` units manage every `/srv/pg/nodeN`). Binaries:
`/usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin` and `/usr/lib/postgresql/17/bin` (17 is first in your `PATH`).
The grader restarts the new server.
hints: Run `pg_upgrade ... --check` first: it tells you what doesn't match without changing anything. Both servers must be stopped. Run it from a directory you can write to (`cd ~`).

The new cluster must be initialised compatibly with the old one, notably the same **data checksums** setting (`pg_upgrade` won't switch them on or off for you). Ask the old one: `node1 -c 'SHOW data_checksums'` (before you stop it).
`pg_upgrade` copies data, not configuration. Compare `/srv/pg/node1/postgresql.conf` with the new one: the port, `listen_addresses` and the libraries the old server preloads.
After the upgrade, `vacuumdb --all --analyze-in-stages` gives the planner rough statistics fast, then better ones. `pg_upgrade` even prints that command.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
node1 -c 'SHOW data_checksums' -c 'SHOW shared_preload_libraries'   # on, pg_stat_statements
initdb -D /srv/pg/node2 --data-checksums -E UTF8 --locale=C --auth-local=peer --auth-host=scram-sha-256
cat >> /srv/pg/node2/postgresql.conf <<'CONF'
port = 5432
listen_addresses = 'localhost'
shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'
CONF
sudo systemctl stop postgresql@node1
cd ~
pg_upgrade -b /usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin -B /usr/lib/postgresql/17/bin -d /srv/pg/node1 -D /srv/pg/node2 --link --check
pg_upgrade -b /usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin -B /usr/lib/postgresql/17/bin -d /srv/pg/node1 -D /srv/pg/node2 --link
sudo systemctl start postgresql@node2
vacuumdb --all --analyze-in-stages
```
**Lesson:** `pg_upgrade` rewrites the system catalogs for the new version and reuses the data files (`--link`
hard-links them: minutes instead of hours, but the old cluster is unusable once the new one starts). The new
cluster must match the old one's checksum setting, so check it before `initdb` (since 16, `pg_upgrade` copies
the old encoding and locale for you). It
doesn't bring `postgresql.conf` or `pg_hba.conf` along, so carry over anything that matters (here
`shared_preload_libraries`). And until PostgreSQL 18, it doesn't bring planner statistics either: analyze
right away, or the first hour after the upgrade is full of terrible plans.
scenarios.narrative:
**Dana:** Production is still on 16, on the cluster Tomás made at a hackathon. Tonight is our maintenance
window: the shop's in read-only mode from 23:00 to 01:00. Get it onto 17.

**Tomás:** Can't we just dump and restore? It's only a few gigs.

**Dana:** Today it is. Learn `pg_upgrade` now, while it's small.

scenarios.title: Locked out
scenarios.summary: The app can't connect to its database. The app config is not yours to change.
scenarios.description:
After a "security hardening" ticket, the billing app can't use its database.
The app connects with the URL in `/srv/app/app.env`; you can read it but **must not change it**.

Make this work:
```
psql "$(grep DATABASE_URL /srv/app/app.env | cut -d= -f2-)" -c 'select count(*) from accounts'
```

Rules: no `trust` authentication for host connections. You are the `postgres` OS user and can
connect as superuser over the local socket with plain `psql`.
hints: Run the command and read the error. Then run it again after each fix: there are several layers.
`select * from pg_hba_file_rules;` shows how Postgres parsed `pg_hba.conf`. Rules are matched top-down, first match wins. Reload with `select pg_reload_conf();`.
Check the role itself: `\\du app` and `select rolcanlogin, rolvaliduntil from pg_roles where rolname='app';`
Connecting is not the same as being allowed to read: `\\dp accounts`.
scenarios.solution:
Four independent locks, each surfaced by the next error message:

1. **pg_hba.conf**: a `host billing app 127.0.0.1/32 reject` line sits *above* the scram line. First match wins.
   Delete it, then `select pg_reload_conf();`.
2. **Role can't log in**: `alter role app login;`
3. **Password expired**: `alter role app valid until 'infinity';`
   (Expired passwords give the same "password authentication failed" error as a wrong one. Check the server log.)
4. **No privilege on the table**: `grant select on accounts to app;` (in database `billing`).

**Lesson:** auth failures are layered: network rule → role attributes → password validity → object privileges.
The client error is often vague; the server log (`/var/log/postgresql/postgresql.log`) says what really happened.

scenarios.title: DELETE without a WHERE
scenarios.summary: Every shipment is gone. Restore them to the second before the DELETE, without losing anything else.
scenarios.description:
On **`node1`** (port 5432), `DELETE FROM shipments` ran without a `WHERE` this afternoon. The server is still up
and other tables kept changing after the accident.

Restore **`parcels.shipments` exactly as it was immediately before the DELETE**: last night's rows *and*
everything created or updated today.

- **`tracking_events` and `customers`** already have changes from *after* the DELETE: they must stay as they are now.
- `node1` keeps running as the production server (same cluster, same timeline). Don't replace it with a restore.
- The production WAL archive **`/srv/wal_archive`** must not get a new timeline from your restore.

What you have: the nightly `pg_basebackup` in `/backups/nightly/` (tar format), the WAL archive in
`/srv/wal_archive`, and node1's log in `/var/log/postgresql/node1.log`. A spare data directory `/srv/pg/node2`
(port 5433) is yours to use.
hints: The plan: restore the base backup into `/srv/pg/node2`, replay the archived WAL up to just before the DELETE, read the shipments from there, put them back into node1.

When did it happen? node1 logs data-changing statements: `grep -n 'DELETE FROM shipments' /var/log/postgresql/node1.log`. Each line starts with a millisecond timestamp. (`pg_waldump` on the archived segments works too.)

Restore: `mkdir -m 700 /srv/pg/node2`, extract `base.tar.gz` into it and `pg_wal.tar.gz` into its `pg_wal/`. In its `postgresql.auto.conf` set `port = 5433`, `archive_mode = off`, `restore_command = 'cp /srv/wal_archive/%f %p'`, `recovery_target_time = '<timestamp> UTC'`, then `touch /srv/pg/node2/recovery.signal` and `sudo systemctl start postgresql@node2`.

Don't promote the restored copy (that's what writes a new timeline's `.history` file). With the default `recovery_target_action = 'pause'` it stops at the target and stays readable: `pg_dump -p 5433 -d parcels -t shipments --data-only | psql -d parcels` after emptying node1's table.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
T=$(grep -m1 'DELETE FROM shipments' /var/log/postgresql/node1.log | awk '{print $1, $2, $3}')
mkdir -m 700 /srv/pg/node2
tar -xzf /backups/nightly/base.tar.gz -C /srv/pg/node2
tar -xzf /backups/nightly/pg_wal.tar.gz -C /srv/pg/node2/pg_wal
cat >> /srv/pg/node2/postgresql.auto.conf <<CONF
port = 5433
archive_mode = off
restore_command = 'cp /srv/wal_archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_time = '$T'
recovery_target_action = 'pause'
CONF
touch /srv/pg/node2/recovery.signal
sudo systemctl start postgresql@node2
node2 -Atc 'select pg_get_wal_replay_pause_state()'        # paused
node2 -d parcels -Atc 'select count(*) from shipments'      # they're back
node1 -d parcels -c 'TRUNCATE shipments'
pg_dump -p 5433 -d parcels -t shipments --data-only | psql -d parcels
sudo systemctl stop postgresql@node2
```
**Lesson:** a base backup alone takes you back to last night. The **WAL archive** is what takes you to *any
second since*: restore the base backup somewhere else, give it a `restore_command`, a `recovery_target_time`
(or `_xid`, `_lsn`, `_name`) and a `recovery.signal`, and it replays history up to that point. Commits after the
target are left out, so a target taken from the statement's start time stops just before the DELETE committed.
Restore to a **side copy** and move only the damaged table back: production keeps everything that happened
after the accident. Keep the copy paused rather than promoted, and turn off its archiving, so it never writes a
new timeline into the production archive. And test this before you need it.
scenarios.narrative:
**Inês:** The tracking page says "no shipments found" for everyone. Every. Single. Customer.

**Tomás:** I was cleaning up old label-only shipments in psql and… I forgot the `WHERE`. In production. 😶

**Dana:** We have last night's base backup and WAL archiving has been on since Tomás set it up. Never been
tested, but here we are. Bring back **every shipment as it was right before that DELETE**, including today's.
And whatever happened *after* the DELETE (tracking events, customer changes) stays.

scenarios.title: A second copy
scenarios.summary: Build a hot standby of production with pg_basebackup, a replication role and a slot, while parcels keep moving.
scenarios.description:
Make **`node2`** (`/srv/pg/node2`, port **5433**) a **streaming hot standby** of **`node1`** (port 5432), which is
taking live traffic right now.

1. node2 streams from node1 using a **dedicated replication role** (not `postgres`, not a superuser),
   authenticated with a password (SCRAM) over TCP `127.0.0.1`.
2. node2 uses a **physical replication slot** on node1, so node1 keeps the WAL node2 still needs.
3. node2 accepts **read-only queries** while it replicates, and stays a standby after a restart.
4. node1 keeps serving the app: restart it if you must, but bring it straight back.

The grader writes on node1 and expects the row on node2 within seconds.
hints: On node1: `SHOW max_wal_senders;`. A primary needs WAL sender processes to stream to a standby, and that setting only changes with a restart.

Create the role with `LOGIN REPLICATION PASSWORD '...'`, and add a `host replication <role> 127.0.0.1/32 scram-sha-256` line to node1's `pg_hba.conf`. The `replication` keyword in the database column is special: `all` doesn't cover it. Then `SELECT pg_reload_conf()` (or the restart).
`pg_basebackup -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5432 -U <role> -D /srv/pg/node2 -X stream -R -C -S node2` copies the cluster, creates the slot (`-C -S`) and writes `standby.signal` plus `primary_conninfo` (`-R`).
node2 is a copy of node1, *including its `port = 5432`*. Change node2's port before `sudo systemctl start postgresql@node2`.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
node1 <<'SQL'
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_wal_senders = 10;
CREATE ROLE replicator LOGIN REPLICATION PASSWORD 'Repl-Parcel-2026';
SQL
echo "host  replication  replicator  127.0.0.1/32  scram-sha-256" >> /srv/pg/node1/pg_hba.conf
sudo systemctl restart postgresql@node1
PGPASSWORD=Repl-Parcel-2026 pg_basebackup -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5432 -U replicator -D /srv/pg/node2 -X stream -R -C -S node2 -c fast
printf "port = 5433\ncluster_name = 'node2'\n" >> /srv/pg/node2/postgresql.auto.conf
sudo systemctl start postgresql@node2
node1 -c 'select application_name, usename, state, sync_state from pg_stat_replication'
node2 -c 'select status, sender_port, slot_name from pg_stat_wal_receiver'
```
**Lesson:** streaming replication needs three things on the primary: WAL senders (`max_wal_senders`, restart),
a role with the `REPLICATION` attribute, and a `pg_hba.conf` line for the special `replication` database.
`pg_basebackup -R` does the rest: a consistent copy plus `standby.signal` and `primary_conninfo`, so the
standby comes back as a standby after any restart. The **slot** makes the primary keep WAL until the standby has
it, so a standby that falls behind catches up instead of needing a rebuild. The flip side is the next chapter.
scenarios.narrative:
**Dana:** After the DELETE, the board asked one question: "what if the server itself dies?" We need a live copy.
`node2` is an empty data directory on the same box for now; we'll move it to its own hardware later.

**Tomás:** I, uh, tuned some replication settings to zero last year to save memory. Shouldn't matter, right?

scenarios.title: The slow dashboard
scenarios.summary: A customer page query got slow, even though 'there is an index for that'.
scenarios.description:
The "my recent pending orders" page is timing out. The query (database `shop`):

```sql
select * from orders
where customer_id = 4242 and status = 'pending'
order by created_at desc
limit 20;
```

The team swears there is an index on `customer_id`. Make this query run in **under 5 ms**
(execution time, for any customer) and stop it from scanning the whole table.
hints: Start with `explain (analyze, buffers)` on the query.
Look carefully at `\\d orders`. Is every index usable?
An index that matches the WHERE *and* the ORDER BY lets Postgres stop after 20 rows.
scenarios.solution:
`\d orders` shows `orders_customer_id_idx ... INVALID`: a `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` failed
half-way and left an index the planner will never use (but every write still maintains it).
The only other index, on `status`, isn't selective enough, so Postgres reads ~1/4 of the table.

Fix: drop the broken index and build one that serves the whole query:
```sql
drop index orders_customer_id_idx;
create index concurrently orders_cust_status_created_idx
  on orders (customer_id, status, created_at desc);
```
(`reindex index concurrently orders_customer_id_idx;` would also make the old one valid, and
work, but the composite index avoids the sort too.)

**Lesson:** check for invalid indexes after any failed concurrent build:
`select indexrelid::regclass from pg_index where not indisvalid;`

scenarios.title: Checkout is frozen
scenarios.summary: Every update to one product hangs forever. Find the culprit and make sure it can't happen again.
scenarios.description:
Customers can't buy SKU `A-100`: the checkout request hangs. This hangs too (database `store`):

```sql
update inventory set qty = qty - 1 where sku = 'A-100';
```

1. Get updates to `A-100` working again (without restarting PostgreSQL).
2. Make sure a session from the **`reporting`** role can never again hold locks
   by sitting idle inside a transaction for more than **60 seconds**.
hints: Who is connected and what are they doing? `select pid, usename, application_name, state, wait_event_type, now()-xact_start as xact_age, query from pg_stat_activity where datname='store';`
`pg_blocking_pids(pid)` tells you who blocks whom.
`pg_terminate_backend(pid)` ends a session. For part 2, look at `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, which can be set per role.
scenarios.solution:
`pg_stat_activity` shows a `nightly_report` session (role `reporting`) in state
**idle in transaction** for ages: it updated `A-100` and never committed, so it holds the row lock.
Other updates queue up behind it (`wait_event_type = Lock`).

```sql
select pid, usename, application_name, state, pg_blocking_pids(pid) as blocked_by, query
from pg_stat_activity where datname = 'store';

select pg_terminate_backend(pid) from pg_stat_activity
where application_name = 'nightly_report';
```
Prevent it from coming back:
```sql
alter role reporting set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';
```
(or `alter system set ...` + `select pg_reload_conf();` for everyone).

**Lesson:** "idle in transaction" sessions hold locks and block vacuum. Always set a timeout.

scenarios.title: pg_wal is eating the disk
scenarios.summary: pg_wal keeps growing on the primary. Find everything that pins WAL, fix it, and cap it for next time.
scenarios.description:
On **`node1`** (port 5432, primary) the `pg_wal` directory keeps growing. **`node2`** (port 5433) is a healthy
streaming standby that must stay that way.

1. Find **every** reason node1 keeps old WAL and remove it, so a checkpoint brings `pg_wal` back down (the
   grader runs `CHECKPOINT` and expects it under **200 MB**).
2. **WAL archiving** to `/srv/wal_archive` must work again (the grader switches WAL and watches it get archived).
3. Set a **cap** so a forgotten slot can never fill the disk again (`max_slot_wal_keep_size`).
4. **node2** keeps streaming from node1 through its slot.

Useful views: `pg_replication_slots`, `pg_stat_archiver`, `pg_ls_waldir()`, and node1's log.
hints: `SELECT slot_name, active, restart_lsn, pg_size_pretty(pg_current_wal_lsn() - restart_lsn) FROM pg_replication_slots;` A slot nobody consumes keeps every WAL segment since its `restart_lsn`, forever.
`SELECT * FROM pg_stat_archiver;` and `tail /var/log/postgresql/node1.log`. Segments waiting to be archived (`pg_wal/archive_status/*.ready`) are never removed either.
`pg_drop_replication_slot('...')` for the dead standby's slot (not node2's). Fix `archive_command` with `ALTER SYSTEM SET archive_command = '...'` and `SELECT pg_reload_conf()`: no restart needed.
`ALTER SYSTEM SET max_slot_wal_keep_size = '1GB'`: a slot that falls further behind than that gets invalidated instead of filling the disk.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
node1 -c 'select slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_current_wal_lsn() - restart_lsn) from pg_replication_slots'
node1 -c 'select failed_count, last_failed_wal, last_archived_wal from pg_stat_archiver'
grep -m3 'archive command failed' /var/log/postgresql/node1.log      # cp: ... /srv/wal-archive/...: No such file or directory
node1 <<'SQL'
SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('node3');
ALTER SYSTEM SET archive_command = 'test ! -f /srv/wal_archive/%f && cp %p /srv/wal_archive/%f';
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_slot_wal_keep_size = '1GB';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
SQL
sleep 5; node1 -c 'CHECKPOINT' -c "select pg_size_pretty(sum(size)) from pg_ls_waldir()"
```
**Lesson:** the primary removes a WAL segment only when **nobody needs it any more**: not a replication slot
(every slot, even one whose standby was deleted years ago), not the archiver (a failing `archive_command` keeps
every segment as `.ready` and retries forever), and not `wal_keep_size`. Monitor all three:
`pg_replication_slots` for inactive slots and their retained bytes, `pg_stat_archiver` for failures. And set
`max_slot_wal_keep_size`: losing a dead standby's slot is much better than losing the primary to a full disk.
scenarios.narrative:
**Inês:** Disk alert on node1: `pg_wal` is almost 300 MB and climbing; it was 40 MB last month.
It only ever goes up.

**Tomás:** We tried a node3 standby a while back, it didn't work out, so I deleted its data directory. Oh, and I
moved the archive folder when I tidied up `/srv`. Probably unrelated?

**Dana:** Find out why WAL isn't being recycled and fix it. **Don't break node2**: it's our only standby.

scenarios.title: The primary is gone
scenarios.summary: node1 died mid-shift. Promote the right standby, get writes flowing, re-home the others and rejoin node1 with pg_rewind.
scenarios.description:
**`node1`** (port 5432), the primary, has crashed and its host is offline. **`node2`** (5433) and **`node3`**
(5434) were its standbys. The app reads its target from **`/srv/app/db.env`** (`DB_PORT`) and retries every
few hundred milliseconds.

1. **Promote the right standby**: the new primary must have **every delivery the app was told was saved**.
2. **Writes must work** on the new primary (the app and the grader both write), and the app points at it.
3. The **other standby** streams from the new primary and is caught up.
4. When node1's host comes back (Inês will tell you, watch `~/`), make node1 a **standby of the new primary**.
   It must never accept writes again as a primary of its own.

In the end: one primary, two streaming standbys, the app writing to the primary. Replication role:
`replicator`, password `Repl-Parcel-2026`.
hints: Which standby has everything? `nodeN -c 'select pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(), pg_last_wal_receive_lsn()'` and `select * from pg_stat_wal_receiver` on each. Is node3 even connected? Read its log.

`select pg_promote()` on the standby you chose. If writes then hang forever, look at what the new primary is waiting for: `SHOW synchronous_standby_names;` (configs are often identical on every node).

To re-home a standby, edit `primary_conninfo` (and `primary_slot_name`) in its `postgresql.auto.conf`. Both reload without a restart, but the slot must exist on the new primary: `pg_create_physical_replication_slot('...')`.

node1 crashed while it was primary, so it may have WAL the new primary never got. `pg_rewind -D /srv/pg/node1 --source-server='port=5433 user=postgres dbname=postgres'` winds it back to the fork point. Then give it `standby.signal`, `primary_conninfo` and a slot, and start it.
`pg_rewind` copies the source's configuration files too: node1 now has node2's `postgresql.auto.conf` (port 5433!). Set node1's `port = 5432` (and `cluster_name`) again before starting it.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
for n in 2 3; do node$n -Atc "select $n, pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(), (select status from pg_stat_wal_receiver)"; done
tail -3 /var/log/postgresql/node3.log            # password authentication failed: node3 is a week behind
node2 -c 'select pg_promote()'
node2 <<'SQL'
ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (node1, node3)';  -- or '' while you rebuild
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('node1');
SELECT pg_create_physical_replication_slot('node3');
SQL
sed -i 's/^DB_PORT=.*/DB_PORT=5433/' /srv/app/db.env
cat >> /srv/pg/node3/postgresql.auto.conf <<'CONF'
primary_conninfo = 'host=127.0.0.1 port=5433 user=replicator password=Repl-Parcel-2026 application_name=node3'
primary_slot_name = 'node3'
CONF
node3 -c 'select pg_reload_conf()'
# ... node1's host is back:
pg_rewind -D /srv/pg/node1 --source-server='port=5433 user=postgres dbname=postgres' --progress
cat >> /srv/pg/node1/postgresql.auto.conf <<'CONF'     # pg_rewind copied node2's config: port 5433
port = 5432
cluster_name = 'node1'
primary_conninfo = 'host=127.0.0.1 port=5433 user=replicator password=Repl-Parcel-2026 application_name=node1'
primary_slot_name = 'node1'
CONF
touch /srv/pg/node1/standby.signal
sudo systemctl start postgresql@node1
node2 -c 'select application_name, state, sync_state from pg_stat_replication'
```
**Lesson:** promote the standby that has **all** acknowledged commits: with synchronous replication that's the
synchronous one, and you verify by comparing replay LSNs, not by trusting what people remember (node3 had been
failing to authenticate for a week, unnoticed). Promotion opens a new **timeline**. Standbys that are behind the
fork point can follow it after you point them at the new primary; the old primary, which may have WAL past the
fork, needs **`pg_rewind`** (possible because of data checksums or `wal_log_hints`) before it can rejoin, and
`pg_rewind` brings the source's config files along, so re-check port and conninfo. Configs
copied to every node travel with the role change: a `synchronous_standby_names` that named the old standby makes
the new primary wait forever for a sync standby that doesn't exist.
scenarios.narrative:
**Inês (03:12):** node1 just went dark. Power supply, I think, I'm driving to the office. The drivers' app can't
save deliveries. You have node2 and node3.

**Tomás (half asleep):** node2 is the synchronous one. node3 is… fine? I rotated the replication password last
week, I think I updated everything.

**Dana:** Get the app writing again without losing a single acknowledged delivery. And when Inês brings node1
back, it must **not** come up as a second primary.

scenarios.title: Two billion events
scenarios.summary: Inserts started failing overnight. The table didn't get any bigger. What happened?
scenarios.description:
Since 03:12 every insert into `events` (database `tracking`) fails:

```sql
insert into events (kind, payload) values ('click', '{}') returning id;
```

Fix it so inserts work again **for years to come**, including tagging new events in
`event_tags`. Keep every existing row.
hints: Read the error carefully. Then `\\d events` and `\\d events_id_seq`.
`serial` means `integer`, and integers stop at 2,147,483,647. Both the column and the sequence have a type.
Who else stores event ids? Look for foreign keys: `\\d event_tags`.
scenarios.solution:
`events.id` is a `serial`: an `integer` column fed by an `integer` sequence, and the sequence hit
2147483647 (`nextval: reached maximum value of sequence`). Rows were inserted with big gaps, so the
table is small but the ids ran out.

Widen everything that holds an event id:
```sql
alter table events alter column id type bigint;
alter sequence events_id_seq as bigint;          -- max becomes 9223372036854775807
alter table event_tags alter column event_id type bigint;
```
Restarting the sequence at 1 is **not** a fix: you'd hit the same wall (and the old ids) again.

**Lesson:** use `bigint` / `bigserial` (or `bigint generated always as identity`) for ids.
On a big production table, `alter column type` rewrites the table under an exclusive lock, so plan for it
(new column + backfill, or a tool like pg-osc). Monitor sequence headroom:
`select seqrelid::regclass, last_value from pg_sequences ...`.

scenarios.title: Vacuum can't keep up
scenarios.summary: Autovacuum runs all day and removes nothing. Find what's holding the xmin horizon back, release it, and keep it from coming back.
scenarios.description:
On **`node1`** (port 5432), autovacuum keeps visiting `parcels.tracking_events` but can't remove its dead rows:
something holds back the **xmin horizon**.

1. Find **everything** that holds the horizon back and release it, so that a plain `VACUUM tracking_events`
   leaves (almost) no dead rows behind. The grader runs that VACUUM.
2. The **reporting** login (`reporting`) keeps working, but an idle-in-transaction reporting session must be cut
   off automatically within **an hour** at most (`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, for that role or wider).
3. Parcelpoint doesn't use two-phase commit: **disable prepared transactions** (`max_prepared_transactions = 0`).
4. node1 keeps running.

Start with `pg_stat_activity` (`backend_xmin`, `state`, `xact_start`), `pg_prepared_xacts`, `pg_replication_slots`,
and `VACUUM (VERBOSE) tracking_events`, which tells you *why* it couldn't remove rows.
hints: `VACUUM (VERBOSE) tracking_events` prints `removable cutoff: N, which was M XIDs old when operation ended` and how many dead rows are `not yet removable`. Something has a snapshot or a transaction ID from long ago.

`SELECT pid, usename, state, xact_start, backend_xmin FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_xmin IS NOT NULL ORDER BY age(backend_xmin) DESC;` A session sitting `idle in transaction` in REPEATABLE READ keeps its snapshot (and the horizon) for as long as it stays open. `pg_terminate_backend(pid)`.
A prepared transaction survives disconnects *and restarts*, and holds the horizon like any open transaction: `SELECT * FROM pg_prepared_xacts;`, then `ROLLBACK PREPARED 'gid'` (or `COMMIT PREPARED`).

`ALTER ROLE reporting SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '15min'` applies to its new sessions. `max_prepared_transactions` needs a restart, and the server refuses to start with 0 while a prepared transaction still exists.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
node1 -d parcels -c 'VACUUM (VERBOSE) tracking_events' 2>&1 | grep -E 'removable|dead'
node1 -c "select pid, usename, state, xact_start, age(backend_xmin) from pg_stat_activity where backend_xmin is not null"
node1 -c 'select gid, prepared, owner, database from pg_prepared_xacts'
node1 <<'SQL'
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE usename = 'reporting' AND state LIKE 'idle in transaction%';
\c parcels
ROLLBACK PREPARED 'billing_migration_step3';
ALTER ROLE reporting SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '15min';
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_prepared_transactions = 0;
SQL
sudo systemctl restart postgresql@node1
node1 -d parcels -c 'VACUUM (VERBOSE) tracking_events' 2>&1 | grep -E 'removable|dead'
```
**Lesson:** VACUUM can only remove a row version that **no transaction could still see**. The oldest snapshot
or transaction ID anywhere in the cluster sets that limit, the *xmin horizon*: a long-running query, a session
left `idle in transaction`, a **forgotten prepared transaction** (it survives restarts), a replication slot's
`xmin`, or a standby with `hot_standby_feedback`. While it's held, autovacuum runs and achieves nothing, tables
bloat and, in the worst case, you head for transaction ID wraparound. Monitor `age(backend_xmin)` and
`pg_prepared_xacts`, cap idle transactions with `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, and keep
`max_prepared_transactions = 0` unless you really run two-phase commit. (The space already lost to bloat comes
back with `VACUUM FULL`, which locks the table, or online with `pg_repack`.)
scenarios.narrative:
**Inês:** `tracking_events` has a few hundred thousand live rows, and the dashboard says almost as many **dead** ones.
Autovacuum runs on it every few seconds and finishes having removed… nothing.

**Tomás:** Could it be the reporting tool? It keeps a connection open all day. Oh, and back in March I tried
two-phase commit for the billing migration. Pretty sure I cleaned that up.

**Dana:** Make vacuum work again, and make sure neither of those can quietly do this to us next time.

scenarios.title: Sorry, too many clients
scenarios.summary: The app can't get a connection. A misbehaving service is hogging all of them.
scenarios.description:
The `web` app (role `web`, password `w3b`) fails to connect to database `app`:

```
PGPASSWORD=w3b psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U web app -c 'select 1'
```

1. Get `web` connected again without restarting PostgreSQL.
2. Make sure the **`metrics`** role can never take more than **5** connections again,
   so it can't starve everyone else.
hints: You (superuser) can still get in, because some slots are reserved for superusers. Who holds the others? `select usename, application_name, state, count(*) from pg_stat_activity group by 1,2,3;`
Free the slots with `pg_terminate_backend()`.
Limits can be set per role: look at `alter role ... connection limit`.
scenarios.solution:
`max_connections` is 15 and 3 slots are reserved for superusers, so 12 are usable, and a leaky
`metrics-collector` holds all 12, idle. Hence `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved...`.

```sql
select pg_terminate_backend(pid) from pg_stat_activity where usename = 'metrics';
alter role metrics connection limit 5;
```
Also worth doing: `alter role metrics set idle_session_timeout = '5min';` and, in real life,
a connection pooler (PgBouncer) in front of chatty apps.

**Lesson:** `superuser_reserved_connections` is your emergency door; per-role connection limits keep
one tenant from starving the rest.

scenarios.title: The empty server
scenarios.summary: Install MySQL 8.4 from the official tarball, configure it, secure it, and create the app's account.
scenarios.description:
Install **MySQL 8.4.13 from the tarball** in `~/downloads` and get it ready for the bookstore app:

1. Unpack it so the server binary is **`/opt/mysql/bin/mysqld`** (basedir `/opt/mysql`).
2. Write **`/etc/my.cnf`** so a plain restart comes back the same: datadir **`/srv/mysql/data`**,
   port 3306, **`bind-address = 127.0.0.1`**, socket `/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock`, error log `/var/log/mysql/error.log`.
3. Initialise the data directory and **start** the server.
4. Set the **root** password to the one in `~/README.md`.
5. Create database **`bookstore`** and user **`'bookstore_app'@'localhost'`** (password in `~/README.md`)
   with full rights on `bookstore` and **nothing else**.
6. Put `/opt/mysql/bin` on your `PATH` (in `~/.bashrc`), so the next DBA isn't confused.

There is no system MySQL here: the tarball is all you have. You're the `mysql` OS user, and `/opt/mysql`,
`/srv/mysql`, `/etc/my.cnf` and `/var/log/mysql` are yours.
hints: Unpack with `tar -xJf ~/downloads/mysql-*.tar.xz -C /opt/mysql --strip-components=1`, then `ls /opt/mysql/bin`.

A minimal `/etc/my.cnf` has one `[mysqld]` section with `basedir`, `datadir`, `port`, `socket`, `bind-address` and `log-error`. Add a `[client]` section with the same `socket` so `mysql` finds the server.
`mysqld --defaults-file=/etc/my.cnf --initialize` creates the data dir and prints a **temporary root password** into the error log: `grep 'temporary password' /var/log/mysql/error.log`.

Start it with `mysqld --defaults-file=/etc/my.cnf --daemonize` (or `mysqld_safe --defaults-file=/etc/my.cnf &`). Then `mysql -uroot -p` with the temporary password and `ALTER USER 'root'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY '...';`
scenarios.solution:
```bash
tar -xJf ~/downloads/mysql-8.4.13-linux-glibc2.28-x86_64-minimal.tar.xz -C /opt/mysql --strip-components=1
echo 'export PATH=/opt/mysql/bin:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc && export PATH=/opt/mysql/bin:$PATH

cat > /etc/my.cnf <<'CNF'
[mysqld]
basedir      = /opt/mysql
datadir      = /srv/mysql/data
port         = 3306
socket       = /var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock
bind-address = 127.0.0.1
log-error    = /var/log/mysql/error.log

[client]
socket       = /var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock
CNF

mysqld --defaults-file=/etc/my.cnf --initialize          # secure: random temporary root password
grep 'temporary password' /var/log/mysql/error.log
mysqld --defaults-file=/etc/my.cnf --daemonize

mysql -uroot -p --connect-expired-password <<'SQL'      # paste the temporary password
ALTER USER 'root'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'lb-root-7Qx2-tarball';
CREATE DATABASE bookstore;
CREATE USER 'bookstore_app'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'lb-app-9Fk3-orders';
GRANT ALL ON bookstore.* TO 'bookstore_app'@'localhost';
SQL
```
**Lesson:** a tarball install is just files, plus a couple of shared libraries the binaries need: on a
real server you'd first install `libaio` and `libnuma` (`dnf install libaio numactl-libs` / `apt install libaio1 libnuma1`),
which this box already has. Beyond that, *you* own the layout (basedir, datadir, config, logs, socket).
`--initialize` (not `--initialize-insecure`) gives root a one-time password; in production you'd also add a
`mysql` system user and a systemd unit. Bind to localhost until you mean otherwise, and give apps a user scoped
to their own schema, never root.
scenarios.narrative:
**Priya (CTO):** Welcome aboard! 🎉 Here's your first server. Nothing on it yet, on purpose: I want MySQL
installed *properly* this time, not `apt install` and hope. The official 8.4 tarball is already in
`~/downloads`. Passwords and the details Marco needs are in `~/README.md`. Ping me when the app can log in.

scenarios.title: Migrated config, dead server
scenarios.summary: Someone copied the my.cnf tuning from the old 5.7 box. MySQL 8.4 won't start.
scenarios.description:
During the upgrade from MySQL 5.7, an engineer copied the old tuning file to
`/etc/mysql/conf.d/`. Now **mysqld won't start**.

Get MySQL running with database `inventory` intact (table `items` must still have its 5000 rows).
Start it with `sudo systemctl start mysql`.
hints: `sudo systemctl start mysql`, then `journalctl -xeu mysql` for what mysqld said. If it says little, look for the error log path in the config.
Where is mysqld trying to write its error log? Does that directory exist, and can you create it?
Some server variables were **removed** in MySQL 8.0. An unknown variable stops the server cold.
scenarios.solution:
Two problems in `/etc/mysql/conf.d/legacy-tuning.cnf`:

1. `log-error = /var/log/mysql-legacy/error.log`: that directory doesn't exist and you can't create it
   under `/var/log`, so mysqld can't even open its log and dies printing to the terminal.
   Delete the line (the main config already logs to `/var/log/mysql/error.log`).
2. `query_cache_size` / `query_cache_type`: the query cache was **removed in MySQL 8.0**;
   `unknown variable 'query_cache_size=64M'` aborts startup. Delete both lines.

```
nano /etc/mysql/conf.d/legacy-tuning.cnf
sudo systemctl start mysql
mysql -e 'select count(*) from inventory.items'
```
**Lesson:** after a major upgrade, diff your config against the removed-variables list, and
`mysqld --validate-config` checks a config without starting the server.

scenarios.title: Access denied, but why?
scenarios.summary: The billing app's account exists and the password is right. It still can't read its data.
scenarios.description:
The billing app connects like this, and the config is **not yours to change**:

```
mysql -h 127.0.0.1 -u app -p'S4fe-pass' billing -e 'select count(*) from accounts'
```

Make that command work. Don't hand `app` any global privileges: it should only be able
to read the `billing` database.
hints: Run the command and read the error. Then run it again after every fix: there is more than one layer.
`select user, host, account_locked, password_expired from mysql.user where user='app';`
`show grants for 'app'@'%';` What does `select current_role();` say when you're logged in as app?
scenarios.solution:
Three layers:

1. **Account locked** (`ERROR 3118 ... Account is locked`): `alter user 'app'@'%' account unlock;`
2. **Password expired** (`ERROR 1820 ... You must reset your password`): an expired password can
   only be cleared by setting it again. Keep the value the app uses:
   `alter user 'app'@'%' identified by 'S4fe-pass';`
   (`password expire never` changes the *policy*, not the flag that is already set.)
3. **Role not active** (`SELECT command denied`): the privileges come from role `billing_reader`, which was
   granted to `app` but is not a **default role**, so it's inactive after login.
   `set default role billing_reader to 'app'@'%';`
   (or set `activate_all_roles_on_login = ON` server-wide.)

**Lesson:** MySQL 8 roles must be *active* to count. `show grants` lists the role, `current_role()` tells the truth.

scenarios.title: Ship it in a container
scenarios.summary: Turn Marco's quick-and-dirty compose file into one you'd trust with real data.
scenarios.description:
Fix **`~/deploy/compose.yaml`** until the reviewer approves it. The rules for a MySQL container we can trust:

1. **Pinned image**: an exact `mysql:8.4.x` version (not `latest`, not just `8.4`).
2. **Data on a named volume** mounted at `/var/lib/mysql`, declared under top-level `volumes:`.
3. **No password in the file**: the root password comes from a Docker **secret** file
   (`MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD_FILE`), and the secret file is readable by you only (`chmod 600`).
4. **Only reachable from this machine**: publish port 3306 on `127.0.0.1` only.
5. A **healthcheck** using `mysqladmin ping`.
6. A **restart policy** (`unless-stopped` or `always`) and a **memory limit**.
7. Tuning lives in `~/deploy/conf.d/*.cnf`, mounted **read-only** at `/etc/mysql/conf.d`.

There's no Docker daemon in this box (it's sandboxed), so the reviewer reads your YAML instead of running it.
Press **Check** any time: it lists everything still wrong.
hints: Run Check early: it lists all the problems. Fix them one by one.

Secrets in compose: a top-level `secrets: {mysql_root_password: {file: ./secrets/mysql_root_password}}`, the service lists `secrets: [mysql_root_password]`, and the env var points at `/run/secrets/mysql_root_password`.
Ports: `"127.0.0.1:3306:3306"`. And inside the container MySQL must listen on all interfaces, or Docker can't forward to it: look closely at Marco's `.cnf`.
scenarios.solution:
```yaml
services:
  mysql:
    image: mysql:8.4.13
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/mysql_root_password
      MYSQL_DATABASE: bookstore
    secrets: [mysql_root_password]
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:3306:3306"]
    volumes:
      - mysql-data:/var/lib/mysql
      - ./conf.d:/etc/mysql/conf.d:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "mysqladmin", "ping", "-h", "127.0.0.1", "--silent"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    mem_limit: 1g

volumes:
  mysql-data:

secrets:
  mysql_root_password:
    file: ./secrets/mysql_root_password
```
```bash
mkdir -p ~/deploy/secrets && openssl rand -base64 24 > ~/deploy/secrets/mysql_root_password   # or any strong value
chmod 600 ~/deploy/secrets/mysql_root_password
sed -i '/bind-address/d' ~/deploy/conf.d/lumen.cnf
```
**Lesson:** containers make the *defaults* dangerous: `latest` changes under you, data in the container layer
dies with it, env-var passwords leak through `docker inspect`, and `3306:3306` publishes on every interface.
Restrict at the port mapping (`127.0.0.1:`), not with `bind-address` inside the container, which would make
the server unreachable through Docker's port forwarding.
scenarios.narrative:
**Marco (backend):** Hey! I need a MySQL I can spin up for staging and on my laptop. I threw together a
`compose.yaml` in `~/deploy` and it works on my machine™. Priya says you have to approve it before it goes
anywhere near real data. Be gentle 😅

scenarios.title: The table that wasn't there
scenarios.summary: Someone dropped the orders table in production. Restore it to the second before it vanished.
scenarios.description:
`bookstore.orders` was dropped this afternoon. The server (`node1`, port 3306) is up and customers are still
being updated.

Restore **`bookstore.orders` exactly as it was immediately before the `DROP`**: every order from last night's
backup **plus every order placed since**.

**Don't touch `bookstore.customers`**: it already has changes made *after* the drop that must survive.

What you have: the nightly dump in `/backups/`, and the binary logs in the data directory (`/srv/mysql/node1`).
`mysqlbinlog` is installed. `mysql` logs you in as root.
hints: The dump was taken with `--source-data=2`: `zcat /backups/*.sql.gz | grep -m1 'CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE'` tells you the binlog file and position it corresponds to.
Find the DROP: `mysqlbinlog -v /srv/mysql/node1/binlog.0000NN | grep -n -i 'drop table'`, then look at the `# at NNN` line just before it. That's your stop position.
Don't restore the whole dump over `bookstore` (that would roll customers back). Restore it into a scratch database instead: strip the `CREATE DATABASE` / `USE` lines and `USE` your own.

`mysqlbinlog --rewrite-db='bookstore->scratch' --database=scratch --start-position=… --stop-position=… binlog.A binlog.B … | mysql` replays the day into the scratch copy. Careful: the rewrite happens *before* the `--database` filter, so the filter names the **new** database. Then move `orders` across.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
cd /srv/mysql/node1
zcat /backups/bookstore-nightly.sql.gz | grep -m1 'CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE'
#   -- CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_LOG_FILE='binlog.000003', SOURCE_LOG_POS=158;
ls binlog.0*                                           # 000003 .. 000006 matter: backup -> DROP
for b in binlog.0*; do mysqlbinlog $b | grep -qi 'drop table' && echo $b; done   # -> binlog.000006
mysqlbinlog binlog.000006 | grep -n -i -B12 'drop table'   # the last "# at NNN" before the DROP = stop position

# 1) the backup into a scratch database (not over bookstore!)
mysql -e 'CREATE DATABASE restore_scratch'
zcat /backups/bookstore-nightly.sql.gz | sed '/^CREATE DATABASE/d; s/^USE `bookstore`;/USE `restore_scratch`;/' | mysql

# 2) replay everything from the backup position up to (not including) the DROP, into the scratch copy
mysqlbinlog --rewrite-db='bookstore->restore_scratch' --database=restore_scratch \
  --start-position=158 --stop-position=<pos-of-DROP> binlog.000003 binlog.000004 binlog.000005 binlog.000006 | mysql

# 3) put orders back
mysql -e 'RENAME TABLE restore_scratch.orders TO bookstore.orders; DROP DATABASE restore_scratch'
```
`--start-position` applies to the first file, `--stop-position` to the last, and `--rewrite-db` is applied
*before* `--database`, so the filter must name the rewritten database (filter on `bookstore` and you get nothing). The scratch copy also gets the
replayed customer changes, which is harmless because you only move `orders` across.

**Lesson:** a dump alone loses everything since it was taken; *dump + binlogs* gets you to any second.
Take dumps with `--single-transaction --source-data`, keep binlogs at least as long as your oldest backup, and
practise this before you need it. Next time, test the restore first: `binlog_expire_logs_seconds` is not a backup policy.
scenarios.narrative:
**Sam (support):** Checkout is throwing errors for everyone. "Table 'bookstore.orders' doesn't exist" 😱

**Marco:** …that was me. I ran the cleanup migration against prod instead of staging. I'm so sorry.

**Priya:** Breathe. We have last night's backup in `/backups`, and binary logging has been on since you set it up.
Get every order back: **including the ones placed today**. And don't wipe out today's customer changes doing it.

scenarios.title: The index that isn't used
scenarios.summary: There is an index on the column. EXPLAIN says it's not used. The query can't change.
scenarios.description:
This query from the order-history page (database `shop`) takes far too long, and it's
compiled into a mobile app, so **you can't change it**:

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_ref = 4242 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
```

There's an index on `customer_ref`. Make the query use an index and examine only a handful of
rows, for any customer. Keep all 400,000 orders.
hints: `EXPLAIN` the query. Look at `type`, `possible_keys`, `key` and `rows`.
Compare the literal in the WHERE clause with the column's type: `show create table orders\\G`.
When MySQL compares a string column to a number, it converts every row's value to a number first.
scenarios.solution:
`customer_ref` is a `VARCHAR`, but the query compares it to the **number** `4242`. MySQL then
converts each row's string to a number (`'04242'`, `'4242 '` and `'4242'` all equal 4242), so it
can't use the index: `type: ALL`, ~400k rows.

Since every value is numeric, store it as a number:
```sql
ALTER TABLE orders MODIFY customer_ref INT UNSIGNED NOT NULL;
-- better still, let the index also serve the ORDER BY:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_cust_created (customer_ref, created_at);
```
`EXPLAIN` now shows `type: ref`, `key: idx_cust_created`, ~40 rows.

**Lesson:** implicit type conversion silently disables indexes. Match column types to how they're queried
(also in JOINs: `INT` vs `VARCHAR`, different collations).

scenarios.title: The migration that froze the site
scenarios.summary: A tiny ALTER TABLE was deployed. Now every query on that table hangs.
scenarios.description:
A deploy ran a harmless-looking migration on database `shop`:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN discount_pct INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;
```

Since then the product pages hang: even `SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = 1` never returns.

Unblock the site **without restarting mysqld**. The migration must finish: `discount_pct` must exist.
hints: `show processlist;` What are the threads waiting for? Which one is the ALTER?
The ALTER is waiting too. For whom? Look at `sys.schema_table_lock_waits` or `performance_schema.metadata_locks`.
A transaction that is *open but idle* holds its locks forever. `information_schema.innodb_trx` shows open transactions and their thread ids.
scenarios.solution:
`SHOW PROCESSLIST` shows the `ALTER` and every `SELECT` in state **Waiting for table metadata lock**.

The ALTER needs an exclusive metadata lock (MDL) on `products`. A `reporting` session ran
`BEGIN; SELECT ... FROM products` and went idle **without committing**, so it holds a shared MDL. The ALTER
queues behind it, and every new query queues behind the ALTER.

```sql
select * from sys.schema_table_lock_waits\G         -- blocking_pid / sql_kill_blocking_connection
select trx_mysql_thread_id, trx_started from information_schema.innodb_trx;
KILL <thread id of the idle reporting session>;
```
The ALTER completes instantly and the SELECTs drain.

**Lesson:** run migrations with a short `lock_wait_timeout` (e.g. `SET SESSION lock_wait_timeout = 5`) and retry,
so a migration fails fast instead of freezing the site. Hunt down idle open transactions.

scenarios.title: A second copy
scenarios.summary: Turn node2 into a live GTID replica of node1, while orders keep coming in.
scenarios.description:
Make **`node2`** (port 3307) a live replica of **`node1`** (port 3306, `bookstore` with live traffic).

1. Replicate with **GTID auto-positioning**, using a **dedicated replication user** (not root).
2. **Seed** node2 with node1's `bookstore` data, consistently, while writes continue.
3. node2 must be **read-only for everyone** (including root), and stay that way after a restart.
4. Both servers keep running; don't stop the writes on node1.

`node1` / `node2` open a root client on each; `systemctl status` / `sudo systemctl restart mysql@node2`; configs are in
`/etc/mysql/nodes/`. The grader writes on node1 and expects to see it on node2 within seconds.
hints: Compare `/etc/mysql/nodes/node1.cnf` and `node2.cnf`. Two servers in one topology can't share a `server_id`, and GTID auto-positioning needs `gtid_mode=ON` + `enforce_gtid_consistency=ON` on both.

Seed with `mysqldump -S /var/run/mysqld/node1.sock --single-transaction --set-gtid-purged=ON --databases bookstore | node2`. The dump sets `GTID_PURGED`, which only works on a replica with an empty GTID history: `RESET BINARY LOGS AND GTIDS` on node2 first.

If the replica's IO thread fails with *Authentication requires secure connection*: MySQL 8's default auth plugin needs TLS or the source's public key. Add `GET_SOURCE_PUBLIC_KEY=1` to `CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO`.
Read-only for root too: `super_read_only`. `SET PERSIST` (or the .cnf) makes it survive a restart.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
# 1. a replication user on the source
node1 -e "CREATE USER 'repl'@'127.0.0.1' IDENTIFIED BY 'Repl-Lumen-2026'; GRANT REPLICATION SLAVE ON *.* TO 'repl'@'127.0.0.1';"

# 2. fix node2's config: unique server_id, GTIDs on
sed -i 's/^server_id .*/server_id = 2/; /^gtid_mode/d; /^enforce_gtid_consistency/d' /etc/mysql/nodes/node2.cnf
printf 'gtid_mode = ON\nenforce_gtid_consistency = ON\n' >> /etc/mysql/nodes/node2.cnf
sudo systemctl restart mysql@node2

# 3. seed: a consistent snapshot that carries its GTID position
node2 -e "RESET BINARY LOGS AND GTIDS"
mysqldump -S /var/run/mysqld/node1.sock --single-transaction --set-gtid-purged=ON --databases bookstore | node2

# 4. replicate, then lock it down
node2 <<'SQL'
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_HOST='127.0.0.1', SOURCE_PORT=3306,
  SOURCE_USER='repl', SOURCE_PASSWORD='Repl-Lumen-2026', SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1, GET_SOURCE_PUBLIC_KEY=1;
START REPLICA;
SET PERSIST super_read_only = ON;
SQL
node2 -e 'SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G' | grep -E 'Running:|Behind|Auto_Position'
```
**Lesson:** GTIDs make the replica's position part of the data: a dump with `--set-gtid-purged=ON` tells the
replica exactly which transactions it already has, so auto-positioning picks up the rest, with no binlog file
and position to copy by hand. Give replication its own least-privilege user, give every server a unique
`server_id`, and make replicas `super_read_only` so nobody "just fixes something" on the wrong server
(spoiler: next chapter).
scenarios.narrative:
**Priya:** After last week, I want a second copy of everything, live. We have one server, which means one bad
disk and we're closed. `node2` is installed but empty. Make it a **real replica** of `node1`, and the shop
stays open while you do it: orders are coming in right now.

scenarios.title: Replication broke at 3 a.m.
scenarios.summary: Someone wrote to the replica. Replication stopped. Fix it properly: no skipped errors, no hidden drift.
scenarios.description:
Replication from `node1` (3306) to `node2` (3307) has stopped.

Get it healthy again, **properly**:

1. Both replication threads running, caught up with node1.
2. node2 holds **exactly** the same data as node1 in `bookstore` (all tables, every column).
3. **No errant transactions**: node2's `gtid_executed` must be a subset of node1's. A replica with
   transactions the source has never seen breaks the next failover.
4. node2 is `super_read_only`, persistently, so this can't happen again.

`node1` / `node2` are root clients. Don't rebuild node2 from scratch: fix it.
hints: `node2 -e 'SHOW REPLICA STATUS\\G'`: read `Last_SQL_Error`. Then compare the conflicting row on both servers.
Fix data on node2 **without writing new GTIDs**: `SET sql_log_bin = 0;` in that session first. Then `START REPLICA;`.
Marco changed more than one thing. `CHECKSUM TABLE bookstore.customers;` on both servers tells you whether a table differs.

Errant GTIDs: `SELECT GTID_SUBTRACT(@@gtid_executed, '<node1 gtid_executed>');` on node2 lists them. Either inject matching empty transactions on node1 (`SET GTID_NEXT='uuid:N'; BEGIN; COMMIT; SET GTID_NEXT=AUTOMATIC;`) or, once node2's data matches, reset node2's GTID history to node1's.
scenarios.solution:
```sql
-- node2: what broke?
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G      -- Error 'Duplicate entry '900001' for key 'orders.PRIMARY''
-- Marco's hand-made order conflicts with the real one node1 later created with the same id.

-- fix node2's data WITHOUT creating new GTIDs on it
SET sql_log_bin = 0;
DELETE FROM bookstore.orders WHERE id = 900001;              -- replication will bring node1's version
UPDATE bookstore.customers SET email = 'reader777@mail.test' WHERE id = 777;   -- Marco's other "fix"
SET sql_log_bin = 1;
START REPLICA;

-- errant GTIDs: transactions that exist only on node2 (Marco's two writes)
SELECT GTID_SUBTRACT(@@gtid_executed, '<paste node1 @@gtid_executed>');   -- e.g. 3e1c…:1-2
```
```sql
-- node1: "adopt" them as empty transactions, so node1's history includes them
SET GTID_NEXT = '3e1c…:1'; BEGIN; COMMIT;
SET GTID_NEXT = '3e1c…:2'; BEGIN; COMMIT;
SET GTID_NEXT = AUTOMATIC;
```
```sql
-- node2: never again
SET PERSIST super_read_only = ON;
CHECKSUM TABLE bookstore.orders, bookstore.customers;   -- on both: identical
```
**Lesson:** `SET GLOBAL sql_replica_skip_counter` or skipping a GTID "fixes" the error and leaves the data
different: silent drift is worse than a stopped replica. Repair with `sql_log_bin=0`, verify with checksums
(at scale: `pt-table-checksum`), and clean up errant GTIDs, because at failover a replica with errant
transactions either can't be promoted cleanly or ships them to everyone. Make replicas `super_read_only`.
scenarios.narrative:
**Sam (on-call), 03:12:** The replica alert is firing. `node2` says `Replica_SQL_Running: No`?

**Marco, 08:40:** Oh no. Yesterday a customer's order was missing from the admin page, and the admin tool was
pointed at node2… so I inserted it there by hand. Also fixed someone's email while I was at it. Sorry!!

**Priya:** Don't just skip the error. I want node2 *identical* to node1 and replication healthy, with no
leftovers that bite us at the next failover.

scenarios.title: Incorrect string value: '\xF0\x9F\x93\x9A'
scenarios.summary: Reviews with emoji fail to save. Accented reviews from years ago must survive the fix.
scenarios.description:
Customers can't post reviews containing emoji (database `shop`):

```sql
INSERT INTO reviews (book_id, author, body) VALUES (1, 'Ana', 'Loved it 📚🔥');
-- ERROR 1366 (HY000): Incorrect string value: '\xF0\x9F\x93\x9A...' for column 'body'
```

1. Make emoji (and any other Unicode) work in `reviews`.
2. Keep every existing review **exactly** as it is: there are years of French and German reviews with accents.
3. New tables created in `shop` should get a 4-byte-safe character set by default.
hints: `SHOW CREATE TABLE reviews;` and `SELECT @@character_set_database` (in `shop`). What is `utf8mb3`, and how many bytes does an emoji need?
`ALTER TABLE … CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci` converts the columns *and* the data properly. Changing only the table default doesn't touch existing columns.
The database has a default too: `ALTER DATABASE shop CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;`
scenarios.solution:
`reviews` (and the `shop` database) use **`utf8mb3`**, MySQL's old 3-byte "utf8", which can't store characters
outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, like emoji (4 bytes in UTF-8).

```sql
ALTER TABLE shop.reviews CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;
ALTER DATABASE shop CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;
```
`CONVERT TO` re-encodes the existing text (é is valid in both, so nothing changes visibly) and switches every
character column. `ALTER TABLE … DEFAULT CHARSET` alone only affects columns added later.

**Lesson:** in MySQL, `utf8` historically meant `utf8mb3`. Use `utf8mb4` everywhere (it's the default since 8.0),
and watch out for legacy schemas: the error appears only when someone finally types an emoji. Converting rewrites
the table, so on big tables use an online schema change tool.

scenarios.title: ERROR 1040: Too many connections
scenarios.summary: The web app can't get a connection. A reporting tool is hoarding all of them.
scenarios.description:
The web app can't connect (it uses `'web'@'localhost'`, password `W3b-Lumen`):

```
mysql -u web -pW3b-Lumen shop -e 'select 1'
ERROR 1040 (HY000): Too many connections
```

1. Get the web app connecting again, **without restarting MySQL**.
2. Make sure the **`reporting`** account can never hold more than **5** connections again.
hints: Why can *you* still log in as root? MySQL keeps one extra connection for accounts with `CONNECTION_ADMIN` (or `SUPER`).
`SELECT user, command, time, state FROM information_schema.processlist ORDER BY time DESC;` and count per user. `KILL <id>` ends a connection.
Limits per account: `ALTER USER … WITH MAX_USER_CONNECTIONS n`.

scenarios.title: The replica is 20 minutes behind
scenarios.summary: Reports show yesterday's numbers. The replica is falling further behind every second.
scenarios.description:
`node2` (3307) replicates from `node1` (3306), and its lag keeps growing. Orders keep arriving on node1.

1. Get node2 **caught up** and keep it caught up (lag under 5 seconds), without stopping node1's traffic
   and without restarting the servers.
2. Make sure the cause **doesn't come back**: the nightly job on node2 must not block replication again.

A heartbeat row (`bookstore.heartbeat`) is updated on node1 every second; on node2 it shows how far behind the
replica really is: `node2 -e 'SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, ts, NOW(6)) AS lag_s FROM bookstore.heartbeat'`.
hints: `node2 -e 'SHOW REPLICA STATUS\\G' | grep -E 'Running|Behind|State'`: what is the SQL thread *doing*?
Who else is on node2? `node2 -e 'SHOW PROCESSLIST'`. Look for long-running sessions and what they hold.
Something holds a global read lock (`FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK`). `KILL` that session. Then look at whoever started it: `ls /srv/backup/`.
`mysqldump --lock-all-tables` takes a global read lock for the whole dump. For InnoDB, `--single-transaction` gives a consistent dump without blocking writers or replication.
scenarios.solution:
```sql
-- node2
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G          -- Replica_SQL_Running_State: Waiting for global read lock
SHOW PROCESSLIST;               -- backup_agent, Query, 1000s: holds FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK
KILL <id of the backup_agent session>;
```
The applier catches up within seconds (the IO thread kept fetching the whole time; only applying was blocked).
Then fix the job that did it, `/srv/backup/nightly.sh`:
```bash
-  mysqldump --lock-all-tables --all-databases ...
+  mysqldump --single-transaction --all-databases ...
```
**Lesson:** lag is usually not "the replica is slow": something is in its way. Read
`Replica_SQL_Running_State`, then the processlist. Global read locks (FTWRL, `--lock-all-tables`, some backup
tools on non-InnoDB tables), long transactions and metadata locks all stall the applier. Measure lag with a
heartbeat (like `pt-heartbeat`): `Seconds_Behind_Source` can lie, especially when the IO thread is behind too.
scenarios.narrative:
**Sam:** The finance dashboard (it reads from the replica) still shows this morning's sales. Is node2 OK?

**Priya:** That dashboard is how we decide restocking for Black Friday. Find out why node2 is behind, get it
caught up, and make sure whatever caused it doesn't come back tonight.

scenarios.title: The CPU is pegged
scenarios.summary: MySQL is at 100% CPU. Find the query that costs the most, with evidence, and fix it.
scenarios.description:
MySQL (database `shop`) has been at 100% CPU since this morning's release. The app is running several
queries in a loop right now.

Find the statement that is costing the server the most **in total**, and fix it so it stops scanning the
table, without changing the app's queries.

Don't guess: the server keeps statistics on every statement it runs.
hints: `performance_schema` aggregates every statement by its *digest* (the query with literals stripped). The `sys` schema makes it readable: `SELECT query, exec_count, total_latency, rows_examined_avg FROM sys.statement_analysis LIMIT 5;`
`sys.statements_with_full_table_scans` lists statements that scan whole tables. Compare *total* latency, not the slowest single execution.
Once you've found it, `EXPLAIN` it with a real value, then add the index it needs.
scenarios.solution:
```sql
SELECT query, exec_count, total_latency, rows_examined_avg
FROM sys.statement_analysis ORDER BY total_latency DESC LIMIT 5;
```
The top entry is `SELECT … FROM orders WHERE coupon_code = ?`: hundreds of executions, each examining all
~300k rows. The `notes LIKE '%…%'` query is slower *per run*, but it runs once a minute, so it's a red herring.

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT id, total FROM shop.orders WHERE coupon_code = 'BF2026-1234';   -- type: ALL
ALTER TABLE shop.orders ADD INDEX idx_coupon (coupon_code);
```
`sys.statement_analysis` then shows the digest's average latency drop to microseconds.

**Lesson:** measure before you tune. `performance_schema` statement digests (via the `sys` schema, or
`pt-query-digest` on a slow log) rank queries by *total* cost: a cheap query run a million times beats a slow
one run once. Fix the top of that list first.

scenarios.title: The primary is dead
scenarios.summary: Black Friday, 09:14. The primary's disk is gone. Promote a replica without losing a single order.
scenarios.description:
`node1` (3306), the primary, is **gone** and won't come back today. `node2` (3307) and `node3` (3308) were
its replicas.

1. **Promote** the replica that has **every transaction node1 committed**. Promoting the wrong one silently
   loses orders.
2. Make it a proper primary: **writable**, **not replicating** from anything, and still writable after a restart.
3. Point the **other replica** at the new primary (GTID auto-positioning) so you still have a copy.
4. Point the **app** at the new primary: `/srv/app/db.env`. The app retries every second, and orders should
   start flowing again once it can write.

Replication user: `repl` / `Repl-Lumen-2026`. `node2` / `node3` are root clients; `systemctl status` shows what's up.
hints: Compare the replicas: `SHOW REPLICA STATUS\\G` on each, especially `Retrieved_Gtid_Set` and `Executed_Gtid_Set`. One has more of node1's transactions (same UUID, higher number).
On the winner: `STOP REPLICA; RESET REPLICA ALL;` (forget the dead source), then make it writable: `SET PERSIST super_read_only = OFF; SET PERSIST read_only = OFF;`.

On the other replica: `STOP REPLICA; CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_HOST='127.0.0.1', SOURCE_PORT=<new primary>, SOURCE_USER='repl', SOURCE_PASSWORD='…', SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1, GET_SOURCE_PUBLIC_KEY=1; START REPLICA;`. Auto-positioning fetches whatever it's missing from its new source.
scenarios.solution:
```sql
-- which replica has more of node1's history?
-- node2: Executed_Gtid_Set: 7b1e…:1-1068      node3: Executed_Gtid_Set: 7b1e…:1-1018
-- node3 stopped fetching a few minutes before the crash. node2 has everything: promote node2.
```
```sql
-- node2 becomes the primary
STOP REPLICA;
RESET REPLICA ALL;
SET PERSIST super_read_only = OFF;
SET PERSIST read_only = OFF;
```
```sql
-- node3 follows node2 and fetches the 50 transactions it was missing
STOP REPLICA;
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_HOST='127.0.0.1', SOURCE_PORT=3307,
  SOURCE_USER='repl', SOURCE_PASSWORD='Repl-Lumen-2026', SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1, GET_SOURCE_PUBLIC_KEY=1;
START REPLICA;
```
```bash
sed -i 's/^DB_PORT=.*/DB_PORT=3307/' /srv/app/db.env      # the app reconnects within a second
```
**Lesson:** failover is a sequence: pick the most advanced replica (GTID sets make that a comparison, not a
guess), detach it from the dead source, make it writable *persistently*, re-home the remaining replicas,
then move the traffic. Every step done by hand under pressure is a step you can get wrong, and doing it at 09:14
on Black Friday is exactly why the next chapter automates it.
scenarios.narrative:
**Sam, 09:14:** EVERYTHING IS DOWN. Checkout fails, the app says it can't connect to the database.

**Priya, 09:15:** I see it: node1's disk died. The hosting company says hours, maybe a day. We have two
replicas. You have the con: get us taking orders again, and **don't lose any**: the last minutes before the
crash were our busiest ever.

scenarios.title: Let the robot do it
scenarios.summary: Set up orchestrator so the next dead primary is handled in seconds, at 3 a.m., without you.
scenarios.description:
Topology: **node1** (3306) primary, **node2** (3307) and **node3** (3308) replicas, GTID. The app writes to
whatever `/srv/app/db.env` says. orchestrator (Percona build, 3.2.6) is installed in `/usr/local/orchestrator`.

1. Create a MySQL user for orchestrator with the privileges it needs to inspect and repair replication.
2. Write **`/srv/orchestrator/orchestrator.conf.json`** (a sample sits next to it): SQLite backend in
   `/srv/orchestrator`, your topology user, **automatic master recovery** for this cluster, promoted replicas
   become **writable**, and a **hook** that points the app at the new primary (`DB_PORT` in `/srv/app/db.env`).
3. Start it (`orcctl start`) and get orchestrator to see **all three nodes** in one cluster.
4. Press **Check**: the grader checks orchestrator's view, then **kills node1**. Within 60 seconds,
   orchestrator alone must promote a replica, re-home the other and run your hook, and orders keep flowing.

`orchestrator-client` is set up (`ORCHESTRATOR_API` points at 127.0.0.1:3000): try `orchestrator-client -c topology -i 127.0.0.1:3306`.
hints: User: orchestrator needs `SUPER, PROCESS, REPLICATION SLAVE, REPLICATION CLIENT, RELOAD ON *.*` and `SELECT ON mysql.slave_master_info`. Create it on node1: it replicates to the others.

Start from the sample, but trim it: `MySQLTopologyUser/Password`, `BackendDB: sqlite` + `SQLite3DataFile`, `ListenAddress: 127.0.0.1:3000`, `RecoverMasterClusterFilters: ["*"]`, `ApplyMySQLPromotionAfterMasterFailover: true`, short `InstancePollSeconds`.

All nodes are on 127.0.0.1, so orchestrator can't tell replicas apart by host in the processlist. Set `DiscoverByShowSlaveHosts: true` (replicas announce themselves with `report_host`/`report_port`) and `HostnameResolveMethod: none`. Then `orchestrator-client -c discover -i 127.0.0.1:3306`.
The hook: `"PostMasterFailoverProcesses": ["sed -i 's/^DB_PORT=.*/DB_PORT={successorPort}/' /srv/app/db.env"]`. `orcctl log` shows what orchestrator is thinking.
scenarios.solution:
```sql
-- node1 (replicates to node2 and node3)
CREATE USER 'orc'@'127.0.0.1' IDENTIFIED BY 'Orc-Lumen-2026';
GRANT SUPER, PROCESS, REPLICATION SLAVE, REPLICATION CLIENT, RELOAD ON *.* TO 'orc'@'127.0.0.1';
GRANT SELECT ON mysql.slave_master_info TO 'orc'@'127.0.0.1';
```
```json
{
  "ListenAddress": "127.0.0.1:3000",
  "MySQLTopologyUser": "orc",
  "MySQLTopologyPassword": "Orc-Lumen-2026",
  "BackendDB": "sqlite",
  "SQLite3DataFile": "/srv/orchestrator/orchestrator.sqlite3",
  "DiscoverByShowSlaveHosts": true,
  "HostnameResolveMethod": "none",
  "MySQLHostnameResolveMethod": "",
  "InstancePollSeconds": 1,
  "RecoverMasterClusterFilters": ["*"],
  "RecoverIntermediateMasterClusterFilters": ["*"],
  "ApplyMySQLPromotionAfterMasterFailover": true,
  "DelayMasterPromotionIfSQLThreadNotUpToDate": true,
  "PostMasterFailoverProcesses": ["sed -i 's/^DB_PORT=.*/DB_PORT={successorPort}/' /srv/app/db.env"]
}
```
```bash
orcctl start
orchestrator-client -c discover -i 127.0.0.1:3306
orchestrator-client -c topology -i 127.0.0.1:3306      # 3306 with 3307 and 3308 under it
```
On Check, node1 dies: orchestrator sees a **DeadMaster** (primary unreachable *and* its replicas agree),
picks the most advanced replica, re-homes the other via GTID, sets `read_only=0` on the winner and runs the hook.
The whole thing takes a few seconds.

**Lesson:** automated failover is only as good as its configuration *and its hooks*: promoting a replica is
pointless if the app keeps calling the dead one. In production you'd run orchestrator itself highly available
(raft), use a proxy or DNS instead of `sed` on a file, persist `super_read_only=OFF` on the new primary, and
rehearse it regularly: an untested failover is a hypothesis.
scenarios.narrative:
**Priya:** Black Friday was heroic. It was also 40 minutes of you typing SQL with the whole company watching
over your shoulder. Next time I want it handled in seconds, even at 3 a.m. Set up **orchestrator** on our
topology. And I want proof: we're going to pull the plug on the primary and watch.

scenarios.title: Binlogs ate the disk
scenarios.summary: The data disk is filling with binary logs. Free space without breaking the replica that still needs some.
scenarios.description:
`/srv/mysql/node1` is filling up with binary logs: nobody ever set an expiry. **node2** (3307) replicates
from **node1** (3306) but is **paused** for maintenance (its replication is stopped on purpose) and will resume later.

1. Remove every binary log that is no longer needed, **without breaking node2**: when node2 resumes it must
   be able to catch up.
2. Never let it happen again: binary logs expire after **7 days at most**, and that survives a restart.
3. Don't delete binlog files by hand: the server must stay consistent with its binlog index.

Leave node2 paused; the grader resumes it to check.
hints: `node1 -e 'SHOW BINARY LOGS'` lists them with sizes. `du -sh /srv/mysql/node1/binlog.*` agrees.
Which file does node2 still need? `node2 -e 'SHOW REPLICA STATUS\\G'`: `Source_Log_File` is the last one its IO thread read.
`PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'binlog.0000NN';` removes everything *before* that file and updates the index. `rm` would leave the index pointing at missing files.
Expiry: `binlog_expire_logs_seconds` (604800 = 7 days). `SET PERSIST` makes it stick.
scenarios.solution:
```sql
-- node2: where did it stop?
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G          -- Source_Log_File: binlog.000031
-- node1: keep that file and everything after it
PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'binlog.000031';
SET PERSIST binlog_expire_logs_seconds = 604800;
```
With GTID auto-positioning node2 asks node1 for the transactions it lacks, and they're all in `binlog.000031`
onwards. Purge past that and node2 fails with error 1236 when it resumes (the hard drill in this track).

**Lesson:** binlogs are both your replication stream and your point-in-time-recovery window. Size the expiry
to cover your oldest backup *and* your longest replica outage, purge with `PURGE BINARY LOGS` (never `rm`),
and alert on disk usage before it's 100%.

scenarios.title: Lock wait timeout exceeded
scenarios.summary: Checkout fails after 50 seconds with a lock wait timeout. Find who holds the lock.
scenarios.description:
Every checkout for SKU `A-100` hangs for 50 seconds and then fails (database `store`):

```sql
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'A-100';
-- ERROR 1205 (HY000): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction
```

1. Get `A-100` updates working again, without restarting MySQL.
2. MySQL has no "idle in transaction" timeout, but it can still close sessions that sit idle too long. Make sure
   an idle session (including one left inside an open transaction) is disconnected after **10 minutes at most**,
   persistently, for new connections.
hints: `SELECT * FROM sys.innodb_lock_waits\\G`: who's waiting, who's blocking, and the ready-made `sql_kill_blocking_connection`.
`information_schema.innodb_trx` shows open transactions and how long they've been running (`trx_started`).
Idle sessions are closed after `wait_timeout` seconds (`interactive_timeout` for interactive clients). Set the global value with `SET PERSIST`.
scenarios.solution:
```sql
SELECT waiting_query, blocking_pid, blocking_trx_started, sql_kill_blocking_connection
FROM sys.innodb_lock_waits\G
-- blocking: a 'batch' session that started a transaction hours ago, updated A-1xx rows and never committed
KILL <blocking_pid>;        -- its transaction rolls back and the locks are released

SET PERSIST wait_timeout = 600;
SET PERSIST interactive_timeout = 600;
```
