**Lesson:** a forgotten open transaction holds its row locks forever, and everyone behind it times out after
`innodb_lock_wait_timeout`. `sys.innodb_lock_waits` finds the blocker in one query. Keep transactions short,
always commit or roll back in `finally`, and let `wait_timeout` reap abandoned sessions.

scenarios.title: ALTER TABLE without the freeze
scenarios.summary: Change a column on a big, busy table with gh-ost, without the shop freezing for a single second.
scenarios.description:
`bookstore.books` on **node1** (3306) has 400k rows and the app updates it constantly. **node2** (3307) is its replica.

Change **`books.isbn` from `CHAR(10)` to `VARCHAR(17) NOT NULL`** and **add an index on it**, with:

1. **No stall**: the app's writes to `books` must never wait more than 5 seconds for a lock. A monitor records
   every blocked write in `/var/log/app/stalls.log`.
2. **No rows lost**, and the change reaches the replica too.
3. **No leftovers**: no helper tables (`_books_gho`, `_books_ghc`, `_books_del`, …) in `bookstore`.

`gh-ost` is installed (`gh-ost --help`). It connects over TCP, and `root` only exists for local socket logins,
so give it its **own MySQL user**.
hints: A plain `ALTER TABLE … MODIFY isbn VARCHAR(17)` has to copy the table, and blocks writes while it does. Try `ALTER … ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE`: MySQL will tell you it can't. That's what gh-ost is for.

gh-ost connects over TCP as `user@127.0.0.1`, so create one (on node1, it replicates): `ALTER, CREATE, DELETE, DROP, INDEX, INSERT, LOCK TABLES, SELECT, TRIGGER, UPDATE ON bookstore.*`, plus `SUPER, REPLICATION CLIENT, REPLICATION SLAVE ON *.*` and `SELECT ON performance_schema.*` (gh-ost checks metadata locks there before cutting over).
gh-ost reads the binlog from a replica by default: point it at node2 (`--host=127.0.0.1 --port=3307`) and it finds node1 by itself. Run it without `--execute` first: that's a dry run.

Useful flags: `--database bookstore --table books --alter "MODIFY isbn VARCHAR(17) NOT NULL, ADD INDEX idx_isbn (isbn)" --initially-drop-ghost-table --ok-to-drop-table --chunk-size=2000 --max-load=Threads_running=25 --critical-load=Threads_running=500 --cut-over-lock-timeout-seconds=2 --execute`.
`--ok-to-drop-table` lets gh-ost drop the old table after the cut-over, so nothing is left behind.
scenarios.solution:
```sql
-- node1: a user for gh-ost (it connects over TCP; root@localhost is socket-only)
CREATE USER 'ghost'@'127.0.0.1' IDENTIFIED BY 'Ghost-Lumen-2026';
GRANT ALTER, CREATE, DELETE, DROP, INDEX, INSERT, LOCK TABLES, SELECT, TRIGGER, UPDATE ON bookstore.* TO 'ghost'@'127.0.0.1';
GRANT SUPER, REPLICATION CLIENT, REPLICATION SLAVE ON *.* TO 'ghost'@'127.0.0.1';
GRANT SELECT ON performance_schema.* TO 'ghost'@'127.0.0.1';
```
```bash
gh-ost --host=127.0.0.1 --port=3307 --user=ghost --password='Ghost-Lumen-2026' \
  --database=bookstore --table=books \
  --alter="MODIFY isbn VARCHAR(17) NOT NULL, ADD INDEX idx_isbn (isbn)" \
  --chunk-size=2000 --max-load=Threads_running=25 --critical-load=Threads_running=500 \
  --initially-drop-ghost-table --ok-to-drop-table --exact-rowcount --cut-over-lock-timeout-seconds=2 \
  --execute
```
gh-ost creates `_books_gho` with the new schema, copies rows in small chunks while **tailing the binlog** to
apply the app's concurrent changes, then cuts over with a brief atomic `RENAME`. The app never waits on a
long lock, and the change replicates like any other statement.

**Lesson:** MySQL 8 does many changes `INSTANT` or `INPLACE` (adding a column is instant now), so check with
`ALGORITHM=INSTANT`/`INPLACE, LOCK=NONE` first: MySQL refuses rather than locks. For changes that need a full
copy (type changes, charset conversions), use a triggerless online schema change tool like gh-ost (or
`pt-online-schema-change`), throttle it on load and replica lag, and keep the cut-over boring.
scenarios.narrative:
**Marco:** We're moving to ISBN-13. `books.isbn` is `CHAR(10)` and it needs to be `VARCHAR(17)` with an index.
Last time I ran an `ALTER TABLE` on `books` the whole site froze for a minute and Sam got 200 emails.

**Priya:** Not again. Do it **online**. Use gh-ost: it's on the box.

scenarios.title: Error 1236: the source purged required binary logs
scenarios.summary: The replica was offline too long. The binlogs it needs are gone. Bring it back.
scenarios.description:
`node2` (3307) was switched off for a week for a hardware repair. Meanwhile `node1` (3306) kept taking orders
and purged its old binary logs. Now node2 won't resume replicating.

Bring node2 back as a healthy, **identical** replica of node1:

1. Replication running with GTID auto-positioning, caught up.
2. node2's `bookstore` data matches node1's exactly, and node2 has no transactions node1 doesn't.
3. node2 is `super_read_only`, persistently.

Orders keep arriving on node1 the whole time: don't stop them. `node1` / `node2` are root clients;
the replication user is `repl` / `Repl-Lumen-2026`.
hints: `node2 -e 'SHOW REPLICA STATUS\\G'`: read `Last_IO_Error`. Compare node1's `@@gtid_purged` with node2's `@@gtid_executed`.
The missing transactions don't exist anywhere any more, so node2 has to be **reseeded** from a fresh copy of node1. (Purging less on node1 next time would have avoided this.)

Logical reseed: on node2, stop replication, drop `bookstore` and `RESET BINARY LOGS AND GTIDS` (temporarily turn off `super_read_only`), then `mysqldump -S /var/run/mysqld/node1.sock --single-transaction --set-gtid-purged=ON --databases bookstore | node2` and `START REPLICA`.

Or physical: the CLONE plugin (`INSTALL PLUGIN clone SONAME 'mysql_clone.so'` on both, a donor user with `BACKUP_ADMIN`, `clone_valid_donor_list`, then `CLONE INSTANCE FROM …` on node2; afterwards start node2 with `sudo systemctl start mysql@node2`).
scenarios.solution:
```sql
-- node2: Got fatal error 1236 from source ... the source has purged binary logs containing GTIDs that the replica requires.
STOP REPLICA;
SET GLOBAL super_read_only = OFF;
DROP DATABASE bookstore;
RESET BINARY LOGS AND GTIDS;            -- forget node2's GTID history
```
```bash
mysqldump -S /var/run/mysqld/node1.sock --single-transaction --set-gtid-purged=ON --databases bookstore | node2
```
```sql
-- node2
START REPLICA;                           -- auto-position continues from the dump's GTID_PURGED
SET PERSIST super_read_only = ON;
```
(The CLONE plugin does the same physically and is much faster on big data sets.)

**Lesson:** GTID auto-positioning can only resume if the source still has every transaction the replica
lacks. Once they're purged, the only way back is a reseed. Keep `binlog_expire_logs_seconds` longer than your
longest planned replica outage, and keep a reseed procedure (dump or CLONE) written down and tested.

scenarios.title: The tutorial's settings
scenarios.summary: Verdant's MongoDB listens everywhere with no auth. Turn on access control with an admin, an app user and a read-only user.
scenarios.description:
**`node1`** (port 27017) runs without access control and listens on every interface. Databases: `verdant` (the
app's) and `billing` (finance only).

1. **Access control on**, listening on **localhost only**. Unauthenticated clients can't read anything.
2. **`admin`** / `Verdant-Admin-2026` in the `admin` database, role **`root`**.
3. **`verdant_app`** / `Verdant-App-2026`: **read and write `verdant`**, nothing else (not `billing`). The app
   connects with the string in `/srv/app/app.env`: **don't change it**.
4. **`verdant_ro`** / `Verdant-RO-2026`: **read-only** on `verdant`, same `authSource` as the app.
5. It all survives a restart (the grader restarts node1).
hints: The **localhost exception**: with access control on and no users yet, a client on localhost can create the first user. Or create the users first and turn auth on afterwards.
Look at the app's connection string: `authSource=verdant` means its user must be created **in the `verdant` database** (`use verdant` then `db.createUser(...)`), not in `admin`.
`roles: [{ role: 'readWrite', db: 'verdant' }]` for the app, `'read'` for the dashboard, `[{ role: 'root', db: 'admin' }]` for the admin.
In `/etc/mongodb/nodes/node1.conf`: `net.bindIp: 127.0.0.1` and a `security:` section with `authorization: enabled`. Then `sudo systemctl restart mongod@node1`.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
node1 --quiet <<'JS'
use admin
db.createUser({ user: 'admin', pwd: 'Verdant-Admin-2026', roles: [{ role: 'root', db: 'admin' }] })
use verdant
db.createUser({ user: 'verdant_app', pwd: 'Verdant-App-2026', roles: [{ role: 'readWrite', db: 'verdant' }] })
db.createUser({ user: 'verdant_ro', pwd: 'Verdant-RO-2026', roles: [{ role: 'read', db: 'verdant' }] })
JS
sed -i 's/bindIp: 0.0.0.0/bindIp: 127.0.0.1/' /etc/mongodb/nodes/node1.conf
printf 'security:\n  authorization: enabled\n' >> /etc/mongodb/nodes/node1.conf
sudo systemctl restart mongod@node1
. /srv/app/app.env && mongosh "$MONGO_URL" --quiet --eval 'db.devices.countDocuments()'
```
**Lesson:** without `authorization: enabled`, anyone who reaches the port is effectively root. Turn it on, bind
to the interfaces you mean, and give every client a user with the narrowest built-in role that works (`read`,
`readWrite`, scoped to one database). A user lives in the database it was created in, its **authentication
database**, which is what `authSource` in the connection string names. Getting that wrong is the most common
"but the password is right!" problem with MongoDB.
scenarios.narrative:
**Lena:** Our new customer's security team asked how our database is protected. I didn't have a good answer.

**Kofi:** It's on a private network! Mostly. And the tutorial said auth was optional for development…

**Lena:** We're not in development. I want an admin for us, an app user that can only touch `verdant`, and a
read-only login for the support dashboard. Ana's dashboard must not be able to change anything.

scenarios.title: mongod refuses to fork
scenarios.summary: A config edit over the weekend and now mongod won't come up.
scenarios.description:
Someone "cleaned up" `/etc/mongodb/mongod.conf` and now **mongod won't start**.

Get it running with all data intact: database `inventory`, collection `items`, 5000 documents.
Start it with `sudo systemctl start mongod`.
hints: `sudo systemctl start mongod` fails; `journalctl -xeu mongod` shows mongod's complaint. Fix one thing, then try again.
YAML is picky about indentation. `cat -A /etc/mongodb/mongod.conf` shows tabs as `^I`.
Where is the data actually? `ls /srv`. Pointing mongod at an empty directory would start it, with no data.
scenarios.solution:
Two problems in `/etc/mongodb/mongod.conf`:

1. A **tab** used for indentation (`cat -A` shows `^I`). YAML forbids tabs, so mongod can't parse the file.
   Replace it with spaces.
2. `dbPath: /srv/mongodb`, but the data lives in **`/srv/mongo`**. Fix the path.
   (Creating an empty directory would start a server with *no data*, which is worse than a server that's down.)

```
cat -A /etc/mongodb/mongod.conf | grep -n '\^I'
nano /etc/mongodb/mongod.conf
sudo systemctl start mongod
mongosh --quiet inventory --eval 'db.items.countDocuments()'
```
**Lesson:** read the startup error, and never "fix" a missing data dir by creating an empty one.

scenarios.title: COLLSCAN on the hot path
scenarios.summary: The 'my pending orders' query reads the whole collection and sorts in memory.
scenarios.description:
The orders page runs this (database `shop`):

```js
db.orders.find({ customerId: 4242, status: "pending" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(20)
```

Make it examine **at most 50 documents** and avoid an in-memory sort, for any customer.
hints: `.explain("executionStats")` on the query: look at `winningPlan` stages and `totalDocsExamined`.
Which indexes exist? `db.orders.getIndexes()`. Does any of them start with `customerId`?
The ESR rule: put **E**quality fields first, then the **S**ort field, then **R**ange fields.
scenarios.solution:
The only indexes are on `status` and `createdAt`, so MongoDB either scans every `pending` order or walks
the whole `createdAt` index. Thousands of documents for 20 results, and possibly a blocking `SORT` stage.

Build an index that follows **ESR** (Equality, Sort, Range):
```js
db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 })
```
Now the plan is `IXSCAN → FETCH → LIMIT`, no `SORT`, and `totalDocsExamined` is ≤ 20.

**Lesson:** an index that matches both the filter and the sort lets the database stop early.

scenarios.title: deleteMany, the wrong one
scenarios.summary: Every Porto device vanished. Restore the right ones from last night's dump without undoing today's changes.
scenarios.description:
On **`node1`** (port 27017), `db.devices.deleteMany({ site: 'Porto' })` ran in `verdant` this morning. It was
meant to be `deleteMany({ site: 'Porto', status: 'decommissioned' })`.

1. Bring back every **Porto** device that **isn't decommissioned**, as it was in last night's dump
   **`/backups/verdant-nightly.archive.gz`** (`mongodump --archive --gzip`).
2. The decommissioned Porto devices stay **deleted** (that part of Kofi's intent was right).
3. Every other device stays exactly as it is now: other sites had **firmware upgrades and new devices today**.
4. Leave no temporary collections behind in `verdant`.

Log in as `admin` / `Verdant-Admin-2026` (authSource `admin`).
hints: `mongorestore --drop` (or restoring over `verdant.devices` wholesale) brings back last night's version of *every* device, losing today's upgrades. Restore to a different collection instead: `--nsInclude 'verdant.devices' --nsFrom 'verdant.devices' --nsTo 'verdant.devices_restore'`.
mongorestore takes the same connection options as mongosh: `--uri 'mongodb://admin:...@127.0.0.1:27017/?authSource=admin'` plus `--archive=/backups/verdant-nightly.archive.gz --gzip`.

From the side collection, an aggregation can pick exactly the documents you want and write them into another collection without touching existing ones: `$match` then `$merge: { into: 'devices', whenMatched: 'keepExisting', whenNotMatched: 'insert' }`.
Then `db.devices_restore.drop()`.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
U='mongodb://admin:Verdant-Admin-2026@127.0.0.1:27017/?authSource=admin'
mongorestore --uri "$U" --archive=/backups/verdant-nightly.archive.gz --gzip \
  --nsInclude 'verdant.devices' --nsFrom 'verdant.devices' --nsTo 'verdant.devices_restore'
mongosh "$U" --quiet <<'JS'
use verdant
db.devices_restore.aggregate([
  { $match: { site: 'Porto', status: { $ne: 'decommissioned' } } },
  { $merge: { into: 'devices', whenMatched: 'keepExisting', whenNotMatched: 'insert' } }
])
db.devices_restore.drop()
db.devices.countDocuments({ site: 'Porto' })
JS
```
**Lesson:** a logical dump can be restored **selectively**: one namespace (`--nsInclude`), renamed
(`--nsFrom`/`--nsTo`) next to the live data instead of over it. From there, an aggregation with `$merge` is a
precise tool: filter exactly the documents you need and insert only those that are missing, leaving today's
versions untouched. Restoring with `--drop` would have been faster to type and quietly undone a day of other
people's work. (And for the future: preview a `deleteMany` with `countDocuments` on the same filter first.)
scenarios.narrative:
**Ana:** The Porto growers' dashboards are empty. All of them. The sensors are still sending data, but the app
says the devices don't exist.

**Kofi:** I was cleaning up decommissioned devices in Porto. I typed `deleteMany({ site: 'Porto' })` and hit
enter before adding the status. 😞

**Lena:** Last night's dump is in `/backups`. Bring back the Porto devices, but only the ones Kofi *didn't*
mean to delete: the decommissioned ones can stay gone. And other sites' devices changed today: don't undo that.

scenarios.title: One is none
scenarios.summary: Turn the standalone into a three-member replica set with keyfile auth, keeping every reading.
scenarios.description:
**`node1`** (27017) is a standalone with access control and all of `verdant`. **`node2`** (27018) and
**`node3`** (27019) are running, empty, standalone.

1. One replica set named **`rs0`** with all three as **voting, data-bearing members** (hosts `127.0.0.1:2701x`):
   one PRIMARY, two healthy SECONDARYs.
2. Members **authenticate to each other with a keyfile**; access control stays on.
3. No data lost: every secondary has all of `verdant`, and a write with **`w: 'majority'`** succeeds.
4. The app's connection string (`/srv/app/app.env`, `replicaSet=rs0`) works as it is.

Admin: `admin` / `Verdant-Admin-2026` (authSource `admin`). Configs: `/etc/mongodb/nodes/nodeN.conf`.
hints: Every member needs `replication.replSetName: rs0` in its config, and with access control on they need a shared **keyfile**: `security.keyFile`. It's a startup setting, so restart each node.
A keyfile is 6 to 1024 base64 characters (`openssl rand -base64 756 > /etc/mongodb/keyfile`), and mongod refuses one that others can read: `chmod 400`.

Plain `rs.initiate()` names the member after the machine's hostname, but mongod only listens on 127.0.0.1. Pass an explicit config: `rs.initiate({ _id: 'rs0', members: [{ _id: 0, host: '127.0.0.1:27017' }, ...] })`.
Run `rs.initiate` on node1 (the one with the data) as `admin`. The empty members do an initial sync from it. `rs.status()` shows their progress.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
openssl rand -base64 756 > /etc/mongodb/keyfile && chmod 400 /etc/mongodb/keyfile
sed -i '/^security:/a\  keyFile: /etc/mongodb/keyfile' /etc/mongodb/nodes/node1.conf
printf 'security:\n  keyFile: /etc/mongodb/keyfile\n' | tee -a /etc/mongodb/nodes/node2.conf >> /etc/mongodb/nodes/node3.conf
for n in 1 2 3; do printf 'replication:\n  replSetName: rs0\n' >> /etc/mongodb/nodes/node$n.conf; done
sudo systemctl restart mongod
mongosh 'mongodb://admin:Verdant-Admin-2026@127.0.0.1:27017/?authSource=admin&directConnection=true' --quiet --eval '
  rs.initiate({ _id: "rs0", members: [
    { _id: 0, host: "127.0.0.1:27017" }, { _id: 1, host: "127.0.0.1:27018" }, { _id: 2, host: "127.0.0.1:27019" } ] })'
sleep 10; mongosh 'mongodb://admin:Verdant-Admin-2026@127.0.0.1:27017/?authSource=admin' --quiet --eval 'rs.status().members.map(m => m.name + " " + m.stateStr)'
```
**Lesson:** a replica set is the unit of high availability in MongoDB: members replicate the primary's
**oplog**, elect a new primary when it fails, and `w: 'majority'` makes a write wait until it can't be rolled
back. Converting a standalone keeps its data: restart it with a `replSetName`, initiate, and empty members copy
everything with an initial sync. With access control on, members prove they belong with a keyfile (or x.509),
and host names in the config must be addresses the members actually listen on.
scenarios.narrative:
**Lena:** The big grower's contract says "no single point of failure". Right now our whole product is one
`mongod`. Kofi set up two more servers last week.

**Kofi:** They're running, empty. I tried `rs.initiate()` on the first one and it complained about the hostname,
so I stopped.

**Lena:** Make it a replica set. The app's new connection string is already in place.

scenarios.title: Authentication failed (but the user exists!)
scenarios.summary: Access control was switched on. The app's user is there, the password is right, and it can't log in.
scenarios.description:
Access control is now enabled on this server. The shop app uses the connection string in
`/srv/app/app.env`, which you can read but **must not change**:

```
mongosh "$(cut -d= -f2- /srv/app/app.env)" --eval 'db.orders.insertOne({sku: "X"}); db.orders.countDocuments()'
```

Make that work. Your admin login is in `~/admin.txt`. Rules: keep access control on, and give `app`
only what it needs in `shop`, nothing cluster-wide.
hints: Look at the connection string carefully, especially `authSource`.
Users live in a database. `use admin; db.getUsers()` then `use shop; db.getUsers()`.
Reading isn't writing: compare the app's roles with what the command does.
scenarios.solution:
`app` was created in the **`admin`** database, but the app authenticates with `authSource=shop`,
so MongoDB looks for `app` in `shop` and finds nothing (`Authentication failed`). And its role was
`read`, while the app also inserts.

```js
// mongosh -u admin -p '...' --authenticationDatabase admin
use shop
db.createUser({ user: "app", pwd: "Ap9-pass-2024", roles: [{ role: "readWrite", db: "shop" }] })
use admin
db.dropUser("app")      // tidy up the stray one
```
**Lesson:** a MongoDB user is identified by *name + authentication database*. `authSource` must point at the
database where the user was created.

scenarios.title: Two Bobs, one email
scenarios.summary: Signup let duplicate emails in. Clean them up and make it impossible from now on.
scenarios.description:
Signup has a race condition, and collection `users` (database `app`) now has duplicate accounts.
Emails are **case-insensitive**: `Bob@Example.com` and `bob@example.com` are the same person.

1. For every email, keep only the **most recently updated** document (`updatedAt`) and delete the others.
2. Make the database itself reject a duplicate email from now on, in any letter case.
hints: Find duplicates with an aggregation: `$group` on `{ $toLower: "$email" }` and count.
Sort by `updatedAt` descending inside each group (`$sort` before `$group`, then `$push` the `_id`s): keep the first, delete the rest.
A unique index enforces uniqueness. For case-insensitivity: either store emails lower-cased, or give the index a collation with `strength: 2`.

scenarios.title: The arbiter can't vote for your data
scenarios.summary: Majority writes hang on a PSA replica set. Bring the secondary back, then replace the arbiter so it can't happen again.
scenarios.description:
Replica set **`rs0`**: **`node1`** (27017) primary, **`node2`** (27018) secondary, **`node3`** (27019)
**arbiter**. node2 went down last night and won't start. The ingest app writes readings with
**`w: 'majority'`** and they time out.

1. Get **node2** running again as a healthy secondary, so majority writes succeed.
2. Then **replace the arbiter**: node3 becomes a **data-bearing**, voting member with a full copy of the data.
   No arbiters left.
3. Make **`w: 'majority'`** the cluster-wide **default write concern**.
4. The ingest app (it uses the replica set connection string) is saving readings again.

Admin: `admin` / `Verdant-Admin-2026` (authSource `admin`). Configs: `/etc/mongodb/nodes/nodeN.conf`.
hints: Why won't node2 start? `sudo systemctl start mongod@node2`, then `journalctl -xeu mongod@node2` and its log (`/var/log/mongodb/node2.log`) say exactly what it doesn't like.

With an arbiter, a 3-member set has only **two** members that can acknowledge a write. Lose either and a majority of data-bearing members is impossible: `w: 'majority'` writes wait (and the primary's cache fills with history it can't discard).

An arbiter can't be converted in place: `rs.remove('127.0.0.1:27019')`, stop node3, empty its `dbPath` (`/srv/mongo/node3`), start it again and `rs.add('127.0.0.1:27019')`: it does an initial sync like any new member.
`db.adminCommand({ setDefaultRWConcern: 1, defaultWriteConcern: { w: 'majority' } })` sets the cluster-wide default; `db.adminCommand({ getDefaultRWConcern: 1 })` shows it.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
sudo systemctl start mongod@node2                                   # "permissions on /etc/mongodb/keyfile-node2 are too open"
chmod 400 /etc/mongodb/keyfile-node2 && sudo systemctl start mongod@node2
A='mongodb://admin:Verdant-Admin-2026@127.0.0.1:27017,127.0.0.1:27018/admin?authSource=admin&replicaSet=rs0'
mongosh "$A" --quiet --eval 'rs.remove("127.0.0.1:27019")'
sudo systemctl stop mongod@node3 && rm -rf /srv/mongo/node3/* && sudo systemctl start mongod@node3
mongosh "$A" --quiet --eval 'rs.add("127.0.0.1:27019")'
mongosh "$A" --quiet --eval 'db.adminCommand({ setDefaultRWConcern: 1, defaultWriteConcern: { w: "majority" } })'
sleep 15; mongosh "$A" --quiet --eval 'rs.status().members.map(m => m.name + " " + m.stateStr)'
```
**Lesson:** an arbiter votes in elections but holds no data, so in a Primary-Secondary-Arbiter set **one**
data-bearing member going down leaves the primary unable to reach a majority of data-bearing members:
`w: 'majority'` writes block, the majority commit point stops moving and the primary's WiredTiger cache fills
with history it must keep. Three data-bearing members (PSS) tolerate one failure with no such cliff. If you must
run an arbiter, know that `w: 'majority'` and PSA don't mix. And the keyfile, like an SSH key, must be readable
only by its owner: mongod refuses to start otherwise.
scenarios.narrative:
**Ana:** Sensor readings stopped saving around midnight. The devices retry, so we've lost nothing *yet*, but
the buffers on the greenhouse gateways fill up in a few hours.

**Kofi:** That's the replica set I built before you joined: a primary, a secondary and an arbiter, to save a
server. The primary is up! Why would writes fail?

**Lena:** Get writes going, and then fix the design so one server going down can't stop us again.

scenarios.title: The readings that never expire
scenarios.summary: There's a TTL index, yet two months of readings pile up. Fix the data types, the index and the ingest job.
scenarios.description:
On **`node1`** (port 27017), `verdant.readings` should only hold the **last 30 days**: there's a TTL index on `ts`.
Yet nothing has expired for about two months. An ingest job (`/srv/app/ingest.js`, re-read every ~20 s) keeps
adding readings.

1. Readings **older than 30 days disappear** (the TTL monitor runs every 5 s on this box), readings from the last
   30 days stay.
2. The TTL index on `ts` expires documents after **exactly 30 days** (2592000 s).
3. Every `ts` is a real **date**: no other types left, and the ingest job writes dates from now on.
4. Keep the `{ device: 1, ts: -1 }` index the dashboard uses.

Admin: `admin` / `Verdant-Admin-2026` (authSource `admin`).
hints: `db.readings.aggregate([{ $group: { _id: { $type: '$ts' }, n: { $sum: 1 } } }])`: the TTL monitor only deletes documents whose indexed field is a **BSON date** (or an array of dates). Strings are ignored forever.

`db.readings.getIndexes()`: read the TTL index's `expireAfterSeconds` carefully. `db.runCommand({ collMod: 'readings', index: { keyPattern: { ts: 1 }, expireAfterSeconds: ... } })` changes it in place.

Fix the ingest job first (`new Date()`, not a string), or it keeps adding strings while you convert. Then convert in place with an update pipeline: `updateMany({ ts: { $type: 'string' } }, [{ $set: { ts: { $toDate: '$ts' } } }])`.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
U='mongodb://admin:Verdant-Admin-2026@127.0.0.1:27017/verdant?authSource=admin'
sed -i 's/ts: new Date().toISOString()/ts: new Date()/' /srv/app/ingest.js
mongosh "$U" --quiet <<'JS'
db.readings.aggregate([{ $group: { _id: { $type: '$ts' }, n: { $sum: 1 } } }])
db.runCommand({ collMod: 'readings', index: { keyPattern: { ts: 1 }, expireAfterSeconds: 2592000 } })
db.readings.updateMany({ ts: { $type: 'string' } }, [{ $set: { ts: { $toDate: '$ts' } } }])
JS
sleep 30; mongosh "$U" --quiet --eval 'db.readings.countDocuments({ ts: { $type: "string" } })'   # strings the job added meanwhile
```
**Lesson:** a TTL index is a background job that deletes documents whose indexed field is a **date** older than
`expireAfterSeconds`. A document whose field is a string, a number or missing is silently kept forever, so a
small change in how an app serialises timestamps turns retention off without any error. Check field types with
`$type`, fix producers before data, convert with an update pipeline (`$toDate`), and adjust TTL settings in
place with `collMod`. Schema validation (`$jsonSchema` with `bsonType: 'date'`) would have caught the ingest
change on day one.
scenarios.narrative:
**Ana:** A grower asked why their dashboard still shows readings from September. Our terms say we keep 30 days.

**Kofi:** There's a TTL index on `ts`, I set it up myself! It definitely worked last summer.

**Lena:** Then something changed since last summer. Make old readings expire, keep the last 30 days, and make
sure new readings expire too.

scenarios.title: Bad file format reading the append only file
scenarios.summary: The box lost power mid-write. Redis now refuses to load its AOF.
scenarios.description:
The host crashed while Redis was writing, and now **Redis won't start**.

Get Redis running again with **append-only persistence still on**, keeping as much data as possible
(there were 10,000 `key:*` keys; losing a few of the last writes is acceptable).
Start it with `sudo systemctl start redis-server`.
hints: `sudo systemctl start redis-server`, then read the end of `/var/log/redis/redis.log`. It tells you exactly what to run.
Since Redis 7 the AOF is a directory: `ls -la /srv/redis/appendonlydir/`. There's a manifest, a base file and an incremental file.
`redis-check-aof` can repair it. Back up the directory first: `cp -a /srv/redis/appendonlydir ~/aof-backup`.
scenarios.solution:
The log says: `Bad file format reading the append only file appendonly.aof.1.incr.aof`.
The AOF has garbage in it, so Redis stops rather than load a possibly wrong dataset.

```
cp -a /srv/redis/appendonlydir ~/aof-backup      # always keep the original
redis-check-aof --fix /srv/redis/appendonlydir/appendonly.aof.manifest
sudo systemctl start redis-server
redis-cli dbsize                                 # ~9,950 of 10,000
```
`--fix` truncates the file at the first bad command, so everything after it is lost. Disabling
`appendonly` would also "start" Redis, but with an empty or stale dataset.

**Lesson:** `aof-load-truncated yes` (the default) only handles a cut-off *last* command; corruption in
the middle needs `redis-check-aof`. Back up before you repair.

scenarios.title: Anyone can FLUSHALL
scenarios.summary: Quickbite's Redis has no password and listens everywhere. Lock it down with ACL users that survive a restart.
scenarios.description:
**`node1`** (port 6379) has Quickbite's data, no authentication, and listens on every interface.

1. Listen on **localhost only** (`127.0.0.1`, optionally `::1`) with **protected mode** on.
2. The **`default`** user is **disabled**: an unauthenticated client can't run anything.
3. User **`admin`** / `QB-Admin-2026`: everything.
4. User **`app`** / `QB-App-2026`: any command on keys (and Pub/Sub channels) matching **`qb:*`** only, and
   **nothing in the `@dangerous` category** (`FLUSHALL`, `KEYS`, `CONFIG`, `DEBUG`, …).
5. It all **survives a restart** (the grader restarts node1), and the data stays.

`node1` = `redis-cli -p 6379`. Config: `/etc/redis/nodes/node1.conf`.
hints: `ACL SETUSER app on >QB-App-2026 ~qb:* &qb:* +@all -@dangerous`: `>` sets a password, `~` key patterns, `&` channel patterns, `+@`/`-@` command categories. `ACL CAT dangerous` lists what you're taking away.
Test without logging in as the user: `ACL DRYRUN app FLUSHALL` and `ACL DRYRUN app GET qb:user:1`.
Disable `default` last (`ACL SETUSER default off`), and from then on connect with `redis-cli --user admin --pass ...` (or `-a`, or `AUTH admin ...` inside).
ACL and `CONFIG SET` changes live in memory. Without an `aclfile`, `CONFIG REWRITE` writes both the settings and the users into the config file. (`ACL SAVE` only works with an `aclfile`.)
scenarios.solution:
```bash
node1 ACL SETUSER admin on '>QB-Admin-2026' '~*' '&*' '+@all'
node1 ACL SETUSER app on '>QB-App-2026' '~qb:*' '&qb:*' '+@all' '-@dangerous'
node1 ACL DRYRUN app FLUSHALL                 # "... no permissions to run the 'flushall' command"
node1 CONFIG SET bind '127.0.0.1 -::1'
node1 CONFIG SET protected-mode yes
node1 ACL SETUSER default off
export REDISCLI_AUTH=QB-Admin-2026
node1 --user admin CONFIG REWRITE
sudo systemctl restart redis-server@node1 && node1 --user admin ACL LIST
```
**Lesson:** Redis trusts whoever can reach its port unless you tell it otherwise. Since Redis 6, **ACL users**
give each client exactly what it needs: key patterns (`~`), channel patterns (`&`) and command categories
(`+@all -@dangerous` keeps `FLUSHALL`, `KEYS`, `CONFIG`, `DEBUG`, `MIGRATE` and friends away from the app).
Disable `default` (or give it a password) so nothing runs unauthenticated, bind to the interfaces you mean,
and remember that runtime changes vanish on restart unless you `CONFIG REWRITE` (or `ACL SAVE` with an
`aclfile`).
scenarios.narrative:
**Maya:** A security scanner found our Redis answering on every interface, no password. Anyone who reaches it
can read every session and `FLUSHALL` the lot.

**Ravi:** It was for the demo! …two years ago.

**Maya:** Give it real users: one admin for us, one for the app that can't do anything dangerous. And make sure
it's still locked after the next restart.

scenarios.title: Everyone's cart is empty
scenarios.summary: A restart wiped Redis. Merge last night's RDB back in without clobbering today's keys, then make it crash-proof.
scenarios.description:
**`node1`** (port 6379) restarted this morning with persistence off and came back empty. Since then customers
have logged in again and filled some carts.

1. **Restore** everything from last night's backup **`/backups/redis/quickbite-nightly.rdb`** that node1 doesn't
   have now. Keys that exist on node1 now are **newer: leave them as they are**. Sessions keep their **expiry**.
2. Make node1 **survive a crash**: the grader writes a key, waits two seconds, `kill -9`s node1 and starts it
   again. The key and all the data must still be there.
3. Keep node1 serving while you work: don't restart it with an empty dataset.

Users: `admin` / `QB-Admin-2026` (`export REDISCLI_AUTH=QB-Admin-2026; node1 --user admin ...`).
A spare instance, **`node2`** (port 6380, `/srv/redis/node2`), is configured and stopped: yours to use.
hints: Don't restore the RDB onto node1 directly: loading it replaces the whole dataset, today's keys included. Load it into node2 instead (copy it to `/srv/redis/node2/dump.rdb`, `sudo systemctl start redis-server@node2`) and copy over only the keys node1 is missing.

`MIGRATE 127.0.0.1 6379 <key> 0 5000 COPY AUTH2 admin QB-Admin-2026`, run on node2, sends one key to node1 *with its TTL* and fails with BUSYKEY if node1 already has it. Loop over `node2 --user admin --scan`.

Turn on the append-only file **at runtime**: `CONFIG SET appendonly yes` writes the current dataset into a new AOF first. Setting `appendonly yes` in the config and restarting does the opposite: Redis starts from the (empty) AOF and ignores everything in memory.
`CONFIG SET` lives in memory: `CONFIG REWRITE` writes it to `/etc/redis/nodes/node1.conf`, so the next start reads the AOF. `appendfsync everysec` loses at most about a second in a crash.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
export REDISCLI_AUTH=QB-Admin-2026
cp /backups/redis/quickbite-nightly.rdb /srv/redis/node2/dump.rdb
sudo systemctl start redis-server@node2
node2 --user admin --scan | while read -r k; do
  [ "$(node1 --user admin EXISTS "$k")" = 0 ] && node2 --user admin MIGRATE 127.0.0.1 6379 "$k" 0 5000 COPY AUTH2 admin QB-Admin-2026
done
node1 --user admin CONFIG SET appendonly yes          # rewrites the current dataset into the AOF
node1 --user admin CONFIG SET appendfsync everysec
node1 --user admin CONFIG SET save '3600 1 300 100 60 10000'
node1 --user admin CONFIG REWRITE
node1 --user admin INFO persistence | grep -E 'aof_enabled|aof_rewrite_in_progress'
sudo systemctl stop redis-server@node2
```
**Lesson:** Redis keeps everything in memory; persistence is opt-in. **RDB** snapshots are compact and great
for backups, but you lose everything since the last one. The **AOF** logs every write (`appendfsync everysec`:
at most about a second lost in a crash), and since Redis 7 it's a base RDB plus incremental files. Turn AOF on
at runtime, never by editing the config and restarting an instance whose data only lives in memory. And restore
selectively when you have to: a side instance plus `MIGRATE ... COPY` brings back what's missing, TTLs included,
without overwriting what's newer.
scenarios.narrative:
**Jo:** Support is on fire. Everyone got logged out this morning and every cart is empty. People are rebuilding
their lunch orders from scratch and they are *not* happy.

**Ravi:** The VM rebooted for patches. Redis came back empty… I may have turned persistence off last year,
for speed. 😬

**Maya:** Jo's nightly backup job saved an RDB last night. Bring back what we lost, but don't overwrite anything
customers have done *since* the reboot. And make sure a crash can never do this again.

scenarios.title: OOM command not allowed
scenarios.summary: The cache is full, and instead of forgetting old entries it rejects every write.
scenarios.description:
This Redis is a **cache** for the product catalogue. Since this morning every write fails:

```
redis-cli set cache:product:1 '{"name":"lamp"}'
(error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.
```

1. Make writes work again. Keep a memory limit: this box has 512 MB and Redis must stay under 200 MB.
2. Make sure a full cache can't block writes again, **and that your fix survives a Redis restart**.
hints: `redis-cli info memory`: compare `used_memory_human`, `maxmemory_human` and `maxmemory_policy`.
What should a *cache* do when it's full? Read about `maxmemory-policy`. Do the cache keys have TTLs? (`redis-cli ttl cache:product:1`)
`CONFIG SET` only changes the running server. `CONFIG REWRITE` (or editing `/etc/redis/redis.conf`) makes it stick.
scenarios.solution:
`maxmemory` is 40 MB with `maxmemory-policy noeviction`, and the cache holds more than that. With
`noeviction`, Redis refuses writes when full instead of dropping old data.

For a cache, evict the least recently used keys. The `cache:*` keys have **no TTL**, so `volatile-lru`
(which only evicts keys that have a TTL) wouldn't help: use `allkeys-lru` (or `allkeys-lfu`).

```
redis-cli config set maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
redis-cli config rewrite        # persist to /etc/redis/redis.conf
redis-cli set cache:product:1 '{"name":"lamp"}'
```
**Lesson:** `noeviction` suits a primary datastore and `allkeys-*` suits a cache. Know which one your Redis is.
Setting `maxmemory 0` would "work" until the kernel's OOM killer arrives.

scenarios.title: NOREPLICAS
scenarios.summary: Writes fail with NOREPLICAS. Give node1 the replica it's waiting for, with its own least-privilege user.
scenarios.description:
**`node1`** (port 6379) has `min-replicas-to-write 1` and no replica, so every write fails. **`node2`** (port 6380)
is running, empty, and meant to be that replica.

1. node2 **replicates** node1 and node1 accepts writes again. **Keep** `min-replicas-to-write 1` on node1.
2. node2 authenticates with a **dedicated ACL user** on node1 that can do replication and **nothing else** (no
   keys, no other commands).
3. node2 is **read-only**: nobody can write to it directly.
4. Everything **survives a restart** of both nodes.

Users on both nodes: `admin` / `QB-Admin-2026` (`export REDISCLI_AUTH=QB-Admin-2026`, then `node1 --user admin ...`).
The app writes as `app` / `QB-App-2026`.
hints: `INFO replication` on both nodes shows roles, links and why a link is down; `tail /var/log/redis/node2.log` too.
A replica needs exactly three commands on its primary: `ACL SETUSER <user> on >password +psync +replconf +ping`. No `~` key patterns at all.
On node2: `CONFIG SET masteruser <user>`, `CONFIG SET masterauth <password>`, `REPLICAOF 127.0.0.1 6379`. Then look at node2's `replica-read-only`.
`CONFIG REWRITE` on **both** nodes: node1 for the new user, node2 for `replicaof`, `masteruser`, `masterauth` and `replica-read-only`.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
export REDISCLI_AUTH=QB-Admin-2026
node1 --user admin CONFIG GET min-replicas-to-write                   # 1: writes need a replica
node1 --user admin ACL SETUSER replica on '>QB-Repl-2026' '+psync' '+replconf' '+ping'
node1 --user admin CONFIG REWRITE
node2 --user admin CONFIG SET masteruser replica
node2 --user admin CONFIG SET masterauth QB-Repl-2026
node2 --user admin CONFIG SET replica-read-only yes
node2 --user admin REPLICAOF 127.0.0.1 6379
node2 --user admin CONFIG REWRITE
node1 --user admin INFO replication | grep -E 'connected_slaves|slave0'
node2 --user admin INFO replication | grep -E 'role|master_link_status'
```
**Lesson:** `min-replicas-to-write N` (with `min-replicas-max-lag`) makes the primary refuse writes unless N
replicas have acknowledged recently: a real safety net, and an outage if the replica isn't there. A replica
connects like any client, so with ACLs it needs a user: `+psync +replconf +ping` is all it takes, no key access.
Keep replicas `replica-read-only yes`: a write that lands on a replica is silently overwritten (or worse,
diverges). And `CONFIG REWRITE` on every node you changed, or the next restart undoes it all.
scenarios.narrative:
**Jo:** Checkout is failing: `NOREPLICAS Not enough good replicas to write`. Nobody can place an order!

**Ravi:** I added a "safety" setting from a blog post last night, ahead of setting up the replica. Then I went
home. The replica part didn't happen yet.

**Maya:** Actually I like that setting: if we can't copy a write, I'd rather not take it. So don't remove it.
Give node1 its replica. Properly: its own user, read-only, survives restarts.

scenarios.title: Which key ate the RAM?
scenarios.summary: Memory jumped overnight. Find the single key using the most memory, without KEYS *.
scenarios.description:
`used_memory` on the session store jumped overnight. Find the **one key that uses the most memory**
and write its name to `~/solution`:

```
echo 'the:key:name' > ~/solution
```

It's a production box in spirit: don't run `KEYS *` (it blocks the server). `SCAN` is fine.
hints: `redis-cli --bigkeys` is a start, but it ranks by *number of elements* per type, not bytes.
`MEMORY USAGE <key>` gives bytes. `redis-cli --memkeys` scans with it for you.
The key with the most items is not necessarily the one using the most memory.
scenarios.solution:
`redis-cli --bigkeys` reports `queue:emails` (a list with 200,000 items) as the "biggest" list, which looks guilty.
But it's 200k *tiny* strings. Measure bytes instead:

```
redis-cli --memkeys            # samples every key with MEMORY USAGE
redis-cli memory usage user:avatars
redis-cli memory usage queue:emails
echo user:avatars > ~/solution
```
`user:avatars` is a hash of 1,500 inline images of ~4 KB each, about 6 MB.

**Lesson:** element count ≠ memory. `--memkeys` / `MEMORY USAGE` measure bytes, and `SCAN`-based tools
don't block the server the way `KEYS *` does.

scenarios.title: Let the robot promote
scenarios.summary: Run three Sentinels so a dead primary is replaced in seconds, and make sure the old one can rejoin afterwards.
scenarios.description:
**`node1`** (6379) is the primary; **`node2`** (6380) and **`node3`** (6381) replicate it. The app asks a Sentinel
for the master named **`quickbite`** before each write.

1. Run **three Sentinels**, `sentinel1..3` on ports **26379, 26380, 26381** (configs in
   `/etc/redis/sentinel/sentinelN.conf`, started with `sudo systemctl start redis-sentinel@sentinelN`), monitoring `node1` as
   **`quickbite`** with a **quorum of 2**. They must see each other and both replicas.
2. A dead primary is noticed within **5 seconds** (`down-after-milliseconds`).
3. The grader then **kills the primary**. Within half a minute a replica must be promoted, the other replica
   must follow it, and the app must be writing to it.
4. When the grader **restarts the old primary**, it must come back as a working replica of the new one.

The nodes have a ready-made ACL user for Sentinel: **`sentinel`** / `QB-Sentinel-2026` (the `default` user is
off). Replication user: `replica` / `QB-Repl-2026`. Admin: `admin` / `QB-Admin-2026`.
hints: A minimal sentinel config: `port`, `daemonize yes`, `pidfile /var/run/redis/sentinelN.pid`, `logfile /var/log/redis/sentinelN.log`, `dir`, `sentinel monitor quickbite 127.0.0.1 6379 2`, `sentinel down-after-milliseconds quickbite 5000`. Sentinel rewrites its own config file, so it must be writable.
With `default` disabled, Sentinel has to log in to every node: `sentinel auth-user quickbite sentinel` and `sentinel auth-pass quickbite QB-Sentinel-2026`.
`redis-cli -p 26379 SENTINEL master quickbite` shows `num-slaves`, `num-other-sentinels` and flags. `SENTINEL ckquorum quickbite` says whether a failover could be authorised right now.

After a failover, Sentinel turns the old primary into a replica of the new one. To replicate it has to authenticate, like any replica. Compare node1's config with node2's: what does a replica need that node1 never had?
scenarios.solution:
```bash
export REDISCLI_AUTH=QB-Admin-2026
# node1 must be able to replicate once it's demoted
node1 --user admin CONFIG SET masteruser replica
node1 --user admin CONFIG SET masterauth QB-Repl-2026
node1 --user admin CONFIG REWRITE
for i in 1 2 3; do
  mkdir -p /srv/redis/sentinel$i
  cat > /etc/redis/sentinel/sentinel$i.conf <<CONF
port $((26378 + i))
bind 127.0.0.1
daemonize yes
pidfile /var/run/redis/sentinel$i.pid
logfile /var/log/redis/sentinel$i.log
dir /srv/redis/sentinel$i
sentinel monitor quickbite 127.0.0.1 6379 2
sentinel auth-user quickbite sentinel
sentinel auth-pass quickbite QB-Sentinel-2026
sentinel down-after-milliseconds quickbite 5000
sentinel failover-timeout quickbite 30000
CONF
  sudo systemctl start redis-sentinel@sentinel$i
done
sleep 5; redis-cli -p 26379 SENTINEL ckquorum quickbite
```
**Lesson:** Sentinel is three (or more) small processes that agree a primary is down (**quorum**), elect a
leader among themselves (a **majority** of all Sentinels) and promote the best replica, reconfiguring the others
and telling clients where the new primary is (`SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name`). Run an odd number of them on
separate failure domains, tune `down-after-milliseconds` to how fast you need to react, and give them an ACL user
on every node. And remember every node can end up as a replica after a failover, including today's primary: it
needs `masteruser`/`masterauth` too.
scenarios.narrative:
**Maya:** Two replicas and still nobody promotes one at 3 a.m. except a sleepy human. We're putting Sentinel in.
Ravi already moved the app to Sentinel discovery: it asks the Sentinels which node is the primary.

**Ravi:** And if no Sentinel answers it falls back to node1. So technically nothing changes until you start them.

**Maya:** I'll believe it when I see it fail over. The grader is going to kill the primary.

scenarios.title: The two-second hiccup
scenarios.summary: Every couple of seconds Redis stalls the whole app. Find the commands blocking the single thread and fix the jobs that send them.
scenarios.description:
**`node1`** (port 6379) stalls regularly. Two background jobs run against it, as scripts you can edit:

- `/srv/app/session-cleaner.sh` (every 2 s) removes logged-out sessions,
- `/srv/app/menu-refresh.sh` (every 15 s) rebuilds the big `qb:menu:all` hash.

1. While the grader watches for about 20 seconds, **no command may take longer than 5 ms** (it sets
   `slowlog-log-slower-than 5000` and resets the slowlog).
2. **No `KEYS`** command may run at all.
3. Both jobs **keep doing their job**: sessions with `status closed` disappear within seconds, and the menu is
   still rebuilt every 15 s (it stamps `_built` in the hash when done).

Login: `export REDISCLI_AUTH=QB-Admin-2026; node1 --user admin ...`. The scripts are re-read on every run.
hints: `node1 --user admin CONFIG SET slowlog-log-slower-than 5000`, wait a bit, `SLOWLOG GET 10`: each entry has the duration in microseconds and the command. `LATENCY DOCTOR` and `CLIENT LIST` (look at `cmd=`) help too.

`KEYS pattern` walks the entire keyspace in one go, blocking everyone. `SCAN` does the same work in small steps: `redis-cli --scan --pattern 'qb:session:*'` prints every matching key without blocking.

Deleting a key with hundreds of thousands of fields frees all that memory before `DEL` returns. `UNLINK` returns immediately and frees it in a background thread; `lazyfree-lazy-user-del yes` makes every `DEL` behave like that.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
export REDISCLI_AUTH=QB-Admin-2026
node1 --user admin CONFIG SET slowlog-log-slower-than 5000; sleep 16
node1 --user admin SLOWLOG GET 10            # KEYS qb:session:* (~8 ms) and DEL qb:menu:all (~15 ms)
sed -i "s/rc KEYS 'qb:session:\*'/rc --scan --pattern 'qb:session:*'/" /srv/app/session-cleaner.sh
sed -i 's/rc DEL qb:menu:all/rc UNLINK qb:menu:all/' /srv/app/menu-refresh.sh
node1 --user admin CONFIG SET lazyfree-lazy-user-del yes     # belt and braces for other DELs
node1 --user admin CONFIG REWRITE
```
**Lesson:** Redis executes one command at a time, so latency is about the **slowest** command, not the average.
O(N) commands over big things block everyone: `KEYS` over the whole keyspace, `DEL` (or expiry, or eviction) of
a huge collection, `HGETALL`/`SMEMBERS`/`LRANGE 0 -1` on big keys, long Lua scripts. Use the `SLOWLOG` and
`LATENCY` tools to find them, iterate with `SCAN`/`HSCAN`/`SSCAN`, free big values with `UNLINK` (or the
`lazyfree-*` settings), and keep collections from growing without bound.
scenarios.narrative:
**Jo:** The app's p99 latency graph looks like a comb: a spike every two seconds, and a bigger one every
fifteen. Customers say the menu "stutters".

**Ravi:** Redis can do a hundred thousand ops a second, it can't be Redis. Can it?

**Maya:** Redis runs commands one at a time. One slow command and everyone waits behind it. Find the slow ones.

scenarios.title: Six nodes, 16384 slots
scenarios.summary: Build a 3-master, 3-replica Redis Cluster and copy every key from the standalone server into it, TTLs and all.
scenarios.description:
**`node1`** (port 6379) is the standalone server with all of Quickbite's keys. **`node4`..`node9`** (ports
**7001-7006**, configs `/etc/redis/nodes/node4.conf`..`node9.conf`) are empty, standalone and running.

1. Turn node4..node9 into **one Redis Cluster**: **3 masters, 3 replicas** (one per master), all 16384 slots
   covered, `cluster_state:ok`, every replica's link to its master up.
2. **Copy every key** from node1 into the cluster, with values and **TTLs** intact.
3. **node1 stays exactly as it is** (same keys): it's the rollback plan.
4. The `app` user can read and write `qb:*` keys through the cluster.

All nodes have the same ACL users (`default` is off): `admin` / `QB-Admin-2026`, `app` / `QB-App-2026`,
`replica` / `QB-Repl-2026`. `systemctl status` lists everything; `redis-cli -c -p 7001` follows cluster redirects.
hints: `cluster-enabled yes` (plus `cluster-config-file` and `cluster-node-timeout`) can't be set with `CONFIG SET`: add it to each config and restart the node. Each node needs its own cluster-config-file name if they share a directory.
`redis-cli --user admin -a QB-Admin-2026 --cluster create 127.0.0.1:7001 ... 127.0.0.1:7006 --cluster-replicas 1 --cluster-yes` assigns slots and replicas. (`REDISCLI_AUTH` works instead of `-a`.)

Replicas in a cluster replicate like any replica: with `default` off they need `masteruser` and `masterauth`. If `CLUSTER NODES` shows replicas but `INFO replication` says the link is down, that's why.

`redis-cli --cluster import 127.0.0.1:7001 --cluster-from 127.0.0.1:6379 --cluster-from-user admin --cluster-from-pass ...`. By default import **moves** keys (MIGRATE deletes them from the source). `--cluster-copy` copies.
scenarios.solution:
```bash
export REDISCLI_AUTH=QB-Admin-2026
for n in 4 5 6 7 8 9; do
  cat >> /etc/redis/nodes/node$n.conf <<CONF
cluster-enabled yes
cluster-config-file nodes-node$n.conf
cluster-node-timeout 5000
masteruser replica
masterauth QB-Repl-2026
CONF
  sudo systemctl restart redis-server@node$n
done
redis-cli --user admin --cluster create 127.0.0.1:7001 127.0.0.1:7002 127.0.0.1:7003 \
  127.0.0.1:7004 127.0.0.1:7005 127.0.0.1:7006 --cluster-replicas 1 --cluster-yes
redis-cli --user admin -p 7001 CLUSTER INFO | grep cluster_state        # wait for ok (CLUSTERDOWN otherwise)
redis-cli --user admin --cluster import 127.0.0.1:7001 --cluster-from 127.0.0.1:6379 \
  --cluster-from-user admin --cluster-from-pass QB-Admin-2026 --cluster-copy
redis-cli --user admin --cluster check 127.0.0.1:7001
```
**Lesson:** Redis Cluster splits the keyspace into 16384 **hash slots** spread over the masters; clients hash
each key (or its `{hash tag}`) to find its node and follow `MOVED` redirects. Multi-key commands only work when
all keys share a slot, so design keys with hash tags where you need that. Cluster mode is a startup setting,
replicas still authenticate like any replica, and `redis-cli --cluster` does the heavy lifting: `create`,
`check`, `reshard`, `rebalance`, and `import` from a standalone server (with `--cluster-copy` if you want to keep
the source as a rollback).
scenarios.narrative:
**Maya:** We launch in Madrid and Barcelona next month. One Redis won't hold the lunch rush of three cities, so
we're moving to Redis Cluster: three primaries, each with a replica.

**Ravi:** I've provisioned six instances on ports 7001 to 7006. They're running, they're just… normal Redis.

**Maya:** Copy everything over, and leave the old server exactly as it is until we've switched the app. That's
our rollback plan.

stories.title: Parcelpoint
stories.subtitle: A PostgreSQL story: from initdb to failover and the vacuum that couldn't
stories.intro:
**Parcelpoint** delivers parcels across Portugal: a few vans, a lot of tracking numbers, and one PostgreSQL 16
server that Tomás set up during a hackathon and nobody has touched since. No backups anyone has tested. No
replica. A config file with comments like `# TODO ask someone`.

Dana just raised a round and hired a DBA. That's you.

Over the coming weeks you'll build their PostgreSQL setup properly: a clean cluster, a major-version upgrade,
point-in-time recovery, streaming replication, a disk that fills up, a dead primary and a vacuum that can't do
its job. Every chapter is a real box with real PostgreSQL servers: you do the work, the grader checks it.
stories.outro: Story complete. Parcelpoint's parcels are safe with you.

acts.title: Act I · Day one
acts.intro: Before touching production, Dana wants you to show her what a properly set-up cluster looks like. Then production gets its overdue upgrade.

acts.title: Act II · Don't lose the data
acts.intro: Tomás set up WAL archiving "just in case" and never tried a restore. Today is the day.

acts.title: Act III · A second copy
acts.intro: One server is one bad disk away from no deliveries. You add a standby, and meet the ways WAL can pile up.

acts.title: Act IV · When the primary dies
acts.intro: 3 a.m., node1 goes dark mid-shift. Promote the right standby, re-home the others, and bring the old primary back without a split brain.

acts.title: Act V · The long tail
acts.intro: Everything works, but the tracking table keeps growing and autovacuum is busy all day. Something is holding the horizon back.

stories.title: Lumen Books
stories.subtitle: A MySQL story: from an empty server to zero-downtime migrations
stories.intro:
**Lumen Books** sells used and rare books online. Twelve people, forty thousand customers, and a
database that Marco installed on his laptop three years ago and copied to a VM "temporarily".

Black Friday is in six weeks. Priya, the CTO, has finally hired a DBA. That's you.

Over the next weeks you'll build their MySQL setup properly: install it, containerise it, back it up,
replicate it, survive losing a server, automate failover and change big tables without taking the
shop down. Every chapter is a real box with real MySQL: you do the work, the grader checks it.
stories.outro: Story complete. You run Lumen Books' databases now.

acts.title: Act I · Day one
acts.intro: Priya hands you a fresh server and a laptop sticker. Time to replace the laptop-era database.

acts.title: Act II · Don't lose the data
acts.intro: Nobody has ever restored a backup at Lumen Books. That is about to change, the hard way.

acts.title: Act III · A second copy
acts.intro: One server is one bad disk away from closing the shop. You add a replica, and learn what can go wrong with it.

acts.title: Act IV · When the primary dies
acts.intro: Black Friday traffic, a dead server, and nobody awake but you. First by hand, then with orchestrator.

acts.title: Act V · Change without downtime
acts.intro: The catalogue needs a new column. The table has millions of rows and the shop can't stop.

stories.title: Verdant
stories.subtitle: A MongoDB story: from an open port to a healthy replica set
stories.intro:
**Verdant** makes sensors for commercial greenhouses: temperature, humidity, soil and CO₂, every minute, from
six hundred devices across five sites. All of it lands in one MongoDB that Kofi set up from a tutorial, with
the tutorial's settings.

Lena just signed two big growers and wants the database to stop being the scary part. That's your job.

Over the coming weeks you'll lock it down, recover from a bad `deleteMany`, turn one server into a replica set,
untangle an arbiter that stalls every write and make old readings actually expire. Every chapter is a real box
with real `mongod`s: you do the work, the grader checks it.
stories.outro: Story complete. Verdant's greenhouses report to a database you built.

acts.title: Act I · Day one
acts.intro: The database answers anyone, and someone just deleted the wrong devices. Two fires before lunch.

acts.title: Act II · One is none
acts.intro: A single mongod is a single point of failure. You build a replica set, then fix the one Kofi built before you arrived.

acts.title: Act III · Keeping it small
acts.intro: Readings are supposed to expire after 30 days. The disk says otherwise.

stories.title: Quickbite
stories.subtitle: A Redis story: from an open port to Sentinel, a latency hunt and a cluster
stories.intro:
**Quickbite** delivers lunch in twenty minutes or less. Sessions, carts, menus, rate limits and the order queue
all live in one Redis that Ravi started with `redis-server --protected-mode no` "just for the demo", two years ago.

The lunch rush is getting bigger every month and Maya has hired someone who knows Redis. That's you.

Over the coming weeks you'll lock it down, make it survive restarts, add replicas, let Sentinel handle
failover, hunt down latency spikes and finally move to Redis Cluster. Every chapter is a real box with real
Redis: you do the work, the grader checks it.
stories.outro: Story complete. Quickbite's lunch rush runs on your Redis now.

acts.title: Act I · Day one
acts.intro: Ravi's Redis answers anyone who asks, and forgets everything when it restarts. That ends this week.

acts.title: Act II · More than one
acts.intro: One Redis is one crash away from an empty cart for every customer. Replicas first, then a robot to promote them.

acts.title: Act III · Fast, again
acts.intro: Every two seconds the whole app freezes for a moment. Find out who's blocking the single thread.

acts.title: Act IV · Outgrowing one box
acts.intro: Lunch rush in three cities. Time to spread the keyspace over a cluster without losing a cart.
